articles.title: Putin orders 3-day pause in airstrikes amid envoys’ visits
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv, the Kremlin said yesterday, as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow to try to revive a stalled push to end Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
The decision was tied to preparations for the envoys’ planned visit to the Ukrainian capital, which Kyiv has said will take place today, he added.
Photo: AP
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on Friday said Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the envoys’ visit and urged Moscow to do the same.
Washington’s push to end the fighting, now in its fifth year, has lost momentum as US attention has been focused for the past six months on its war with Iran. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner was in January, when they met with Putin in the Kremlin.
The envoys were met yesterday at the airport by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Tass reported.
Dmitriev shared photos of him greeting the US delegation as they disembarked, alongside the caption: “Welcome to Moscow Peacemakers.”
With peace efforts stalled, Russia had intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with relentless bombardments recently stretching into daylight hours, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of air defensive systems.
On Friday, a Russian drone hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv — the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, which is one of the agencies involved in carrying out deep-strike operations inside Russia.
The long-range strikes by Ukraine have hit Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce hubs, seeking to undermine the Kremlin’s war effort and economy, as well as make ordinary citizens feel the consequences of the war.
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the front line. Russia has been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

articles.title: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
articles.body:
In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile.
But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary.
Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy.
The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more.
Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East.
While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents.
“The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.”
Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.”
After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple.
The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party.
Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation.
The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year
The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long.
The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post.
‘The past six months has failed’
“I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after?
“We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability.
“We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.”
Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade.
“It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength.
As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions.
The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May,
has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination.
In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets.
The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”.
Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts.
A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank.
In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN.
Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis.
The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain.
Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.”
Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said.
‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld
Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war.
Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the International Monetary Fund.
During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein.
But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth.
“Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now.
“But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat.
“If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.”
Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced.
He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa.
“We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.”
Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.”

articles.title: Putin Pauses Strikes on Kyiv as Trump Envoys Visit Russia and Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight on Sept. 6. The temporary pause coincides with a visit from U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
“Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told state media early Saturday. Ukrainian media had previously reported that its army would observe a ceasefire during the visit, though the details had not yet been finalized. "Such information did come from Ukraine,” Peskov confirmed.
Witkoff and Kushner touched down in Moscow later that day to meet with Putin and discuss ending the war with Ukraine. They are scheduled to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday.
Both men are real estate developers whom Trump has used as envoys in high-level diplomatic talks. Kushner is also the President’s son-in-law and served as a senior adviser during his first term.
“They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, calling the two “great negotiators.”
The U.S. served as a primary mediator between Russia and Ukraine in 2025 and into 2026. The envoys’ arrival represents a potential revival of that role, which largely stalled in February when Washington and Jerusalem launched joint strikes on Iran, killing the country’s leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and igniting an ongoing war.
Following the Kremlin’s announcement, Zelensky wrote on X that he had been in touch with the envoys and was “ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process.”
“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,” he wrote, adding that Ukraine is ready for “substantive conversation.”
Hours earlier, however, Zelensky posted about an overnight wave of Russian attacks that targeted major airports in Kyiv and Boryspil and killed five people at an industrial site elsewhere in Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian air force, Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 attack drones in the attack.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelensky said.
Trump attempts to revive stalled Ukraine-Russia peace talks
Trump has repeatedly stated that ending the Russia-Ukraine war is a major priority of his Administration, but the reality of that aim has proven difficult.
In August 2025, the U.S. President met his Russian counterpart in Anchorage, Alaska, to pursue a ceasefire agreement. The talks proved unsuccessful, and Trump left empty-handed.
In October 2025, Trump and Putin planned to meet in Budapest in hopes of furthering peace talks. But the summit was canceled just a few days after the summit was announced after Russia indicated that its hard-line stance on the war had not shifted.
“It just didn’t feel right to me,” Trump said at the time. “It didn’t feel like we were going to get to the place we have to get. So I canceled it.”
Strain between Trump and Zelensky also impeded progress. In February 2025, Oval Office talks collapsed within minutes when the U.S. President accused Zelensky of being “ungrateful” for U.S. aid and refusing to agree to a ceasefire without security assurances. In the 18 months since, however, that tension has largely dissipated, with Trump saying at this year’s NATO summit that the two had “actually developed a good relationship.”
The revived push for peace talks comes days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow last week and met with his Russian intelligence counterparts, a trip that Trump later called “semi-routine,” though it had not been announced to the media in advance and little is known about what transpired.
Renewed mediation comes as Ukraine continues to launch some of its largest aerial assaults of the war yet, showcasing the nation’s rapid advancement of drone and missile capabilities in recent months.
It demonstrated its growing capacity to strike deep inside Russian territory in August, with strikes landing up to 1,500 miles over the shared border—including attacks on warehouses used by the prominent online retailer Wildberries, after Kyiv said its logistics sites are being used to support the Russian military.

articles.title: US Envoys Arrive In Moscow; Putin Orders Halt In Kyiv Strikes As Attacks Continue Elsewhere
articles.body:
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in Moscow as part of a renewed White House effort to end Russia's war against Ukraine, with the pair set to visit Kyiv afterward.
The Kremlin said Russian President Vladimir Putin would receive the two envoys on September 5. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin ordered a three-day halt to Russian strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight ahead of their planned visit to the Ukrainian capital, which Russia has hammered with attacks for a week.
The developments came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of deliberately targeting Kyiv's two airports in overnight strikes in an attempt to disrupt the US envoys' visit. Other Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least five people.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters at the White House on September 4.
He gave no details. Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.
Responding to increasing concerns in the West that Russia could attack a NATO member to test the alliance's resolve, Trump again said he doesn't believe Putin is planning such a move.
"I speak to him. I know him very well. Putin's not looking to attack NATO territory," Trump said.
Zelenskyy said on September 4 that "today it has been clearly determined that American representatives will be in Ukraine and in Russia in the coming days" and he called for a pause in air strikes by both sides to facilitate any meetings.
He added that the US team had informed him that Witkoff and Kushner would visit Kyiv on September 6, a day after their talks in Moscow.
Zelenskyy Calls For Pause In Air Strikes
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces would "ensure the normal functioning of Russia airspace so that the negotiators can arrive there safely" and demanded that Moscow reciprocate.
"There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must also refrain from conducting air strikes for the time needed to hold these negotiations."
Putin's order for a halt to strikes on Kyiv from September 6-8 came the following day. Peskov made no mention of other parts of Ukraine when he told Russian media about the decision, which came amid reports that Russia continued its attacks elsewhere in Ukraine ahead of the planned pause.
Zelenskyy said on September 5 that Russian forces had targeted Kyiv's Zhulyany and Boryspil airports, accusing Moscow of seeking to create uncertainty over the US envoys' planned journey to Ukraine.
"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said on X , adding there would be "no threats to diplomacy" from the Ukrainian side.
Flying into Kyiv would be highly unusual. Ukrainian airspace has been closed to regular civilian flights since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and visiting foreign leaders and officials have generally reached the capital by train.
The visit would come just days after a Russian drone strike hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service -- known as the SBU and a key agency that would be responsible for the US envoys' safety during a visit.
Despite Zelenskyy's call for a mutual pause ahead of a fresh round of diplomacy, Russia continued to target places across Ukraine on September 5, killing five people and wounding five at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, according to regional authorities.
Two people were also wounded in the Kyiv region and two others in the southern Mykolayiv region, according to reports. The Ukrainian military said that, in its overnight strikes, Moscow used Iskander-M ballistic missiles and at least 167 drones, around half of which were jet-powered.
New Diplomatic Push
The US envoys' visit to Kyiv would mark their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and come amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.
Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.
Despite the renewed diplomacy, fundamental differences between Moscow and Kyiv remain. The Kremlin said on September 4 that Putin's position that Ukraine should cede the entirety of the four mainland regions claimed by Russia -- Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhya, and Kherson -- and abandon its ambition to join NATO remained "unshakeable."
Kyiv has voiced willingness to hold talks with the front lines frozen in place, but has repeatedly rejected giving up its territory to Russia and has insisted on security guarantees as part of any peace settlement.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe on August 25 met with the heads of the Russian intelligence and security services in Moscow. The US spy agency did not disclose the full agenda, but the Kremlin said Ratcliffe did not meet with Putin.
Analysts say Washington's broader approach to the conflict remains difficult to discern.
Heather Conley, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute (AEI) and a former senior State Department official, said "it's not clear if the US is willing to place pressure, more pressure on Russia," citing confusion over a Russian sanctions bill currently on an uncertain course in the US Congress and uncertainty over potential licensing of the production of Patriot missiles to Ukraine.
"There's just a lack of clarity right now on on how the US is planning to proceed," she added.

articles.title: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner land in Moscow aiming to revive Ukraine talks
articles.body:
The US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Moscow to try to resuscitate a deal to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as both sides said they would halt airstrikes for the visit.
The envoys were met at the airport on Saturday by the Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, a key interlocutor for the Trump administration’s efforts to end the Ukraine-Russia war. The US outlet Axios reported that they were expected to meet the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, later in the day. 
  The visit came as Trump suggested on Friday a new proposal to end the war, without providing any details on what his new plan might be. Trump made ending the war a priority early in his second term, but his efforts have so far yielded little results.
“I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They’ve done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it,” Trump said.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Kyiv would stop its airstrikes during the US officials’ visit and asked Moscow do the same. The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Saturday that Putin had ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv.
Large gaps remain between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war. On Friday, the Kremlin said it was sticking by the position Putin set out two years earlier – that Ukraine should give up four regions claimed by Russia and not join Nato. That position is intolerable to Ukraine.
Witkoff and Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv on Sunday, which would be the first time the two envoys have visited the Ukrainian capital. Both have visited Moscow before, most recently in January when they met Putin in the Kremlin.
As peace efforts floundered in recent months, with US attention turned to its war with Iran, the conflict has intensified. Ground troops have been locked in a grinding stalemate along the 775-mile (1,250km) frontline with little advances on either side. Both sides have intensified their aerial attacks in recent weeks, hitting increasingly distant targets.
Ukraine has carried out long-range strikes on Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses, to try to degrade Russia’s war effort and economy. Its strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and rising prices at the pump.
On Friday, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), one of the agencies responsible for carrying out deep-strike operations in Russia. Zelenskyy has vowed to retaliate. Russia has also increased its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with waves of bombardments, stretching Ukraine’s air defence systems.
Zelenskyy accused Russia of trying to disrupt the envoys’ visit to Ukraine with strikes on Kyiv’s two airports overnight. “Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. 
 Officials visiting Ukraine have largely done so by train, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 due to the war.
On Friday, Russia carried out overnight strikes, killing five people and wounding five more at a factory in the southern Dnipropetrovsk region, according to the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. He said those killed were employees working at the factory who were “doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.”
A 62-year-old man was injured and several homes and a building were damaged in another attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.
Russia also struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging the building and injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl. Emergency services said they were repeatedly forced to withdraw because of the threat of more strikes.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones overnight, including jet-powered UAVs. Ukrainian air defences disabled 128 of the drones, the air force said.
Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

articles.title: Drone hysteria, Kiev gunfights, and aviation threats: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Drone hysteria, Kiev gunfights, and aviation threats: RT stories that shaped the week
Europe sees Russian drones everywhere
Germany found a new Russian threat this week, accusing Russia of staging a drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, where an explosives-laden UAV was reportedly found between Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft.
Before returning to Germany, RT India reports on a case of Ukrainian mercenaries who launched a drone at a passenger jet in Myanmar, and are now languishing in an Indian jail.
Berlin launched a raft of anti-Russian measures, including closing Moscow’s consulate in Bonn, ending the lease of the Russian House cultural center in Berlin, tightening border controls for Russian nationals, and drawing up another sanctions list.
But as these stories usually go, Berlin presented no actual proof that Russia had anything to do with the drone.
“Where is the evidence? Well, they planted the evidence,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday, suggesting that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz needs the image of an “aggressive Russia” to distract from factory closures, job losses, and falling living standards at home.
Berlin’s outburst is the latest evidence of the mass Russian drone hysteria that has gripped many of Kiev’s European backers. No claims of Russian drones over airports, military bases, and infrastructure have been proven, while the Brussels hymn sheet includes ‘hybrid attacks’ and a ‘drone wall’.
The fact that no investigators have confirmed any of the numerous claims, nor produced any evidence of hostile drone activity, has remained conveniently ignored in the Western mainstream.
Kiev gets desperate, threatens EVERYONE
While European governments searched the skies for Russian drones that may or may not exist, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky threw subtlety out the window and issued a direct threat to virtually all aircraft flying in Russia’s airspace.
”The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky declared on Tuesday, warning “every airline” using Russian airspace that Kiev’s expanding long-range campaign would make flying increasingly dangerous.
After threatening not only Russian passengers, but also airlines from Türkiye, China, the Gulf, Central Asia, and even Europe, Kiev demanded that the International Civil Aviation Organization effectively close Russian airspace to all international traffic. The ICAO did not oblige.
RT looked at who exactly Zelensky was threatening, how many people use Russia’s skies daily, whether Kiev could actually close Russia’s enormous airspace, and why foreign airlines have so far refused to panic.
Russian President Vladimir Putin called out Zelensky’s threats as a blatant move toward “state terrorism,” which calls into question the prospects for future dialogue. “There are no negotiations with terrorists,” he said, warning that Russia would respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in tragedy.
Aviation expert Roman Gusarov told RT that Zelensky’s threat is an “act of desperation” after weeks of punishing Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports, energy facilities, warehouses, and military infrastructure.
Domestic issues keep mounting for Zelensky
Over the week, Zelensky’s problems at home only grew as agents of the SBU and HUR, two of the country’s most powerful security agencies, exchanged gunfire in a residential district of the Ukrainian capital. The shootout took place over the detention of an officer from the neo-Nazi-linked Russian Volunteer Corps. Three servicemen were wounded.
Meanwhile, in Kiev’s suburbs, residents have been demanding answers as to why their government is storing explosives beside their homes. The protests came after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian ammunition depot in the village of Milaya triggered hours of secondary explosions, scattering ordnance throughout the surrounding residential area, killing at least 38 people and damaging more than 200 homes.
Ukraine’s drone raids targeting Russian energy infrastructure also got on Washington’s nerves this week. While Kiev has spent months presenting attacks on Russian oil infrastructure as a way to hurt the Russian economy, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the strikes are rattling the global energy market.
”Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products,” Bessent said, adding that the strikes are creating “upward price pressure on a global basis.”
West aids Kiev’s hunt for Russian property
The Norwegian authorities seized the Professor Molchanov while it was docked in Barentsburg, Svalbard, following a request from Ukraine’s state-owned gas company, Naftogaz, which is trying to shake Russia down for $4.22 billion over supposed lost assets in Crimea.
Check out RT’s detailed explainer to learn more about the ship, its significance for science and Arctic researchers, and the broader context of the arrest.
Russia decried the move as a manifestation of “state terrorism” and has vowed to challenge the seizure in court.
The West escalates, Eurasia shakes hands
The capture of the Professor Molchanov came just days after Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov published a sweeping article on the future of the Arctic, in which he accused NATO of trying to turn the region into a new front against Russia, pointing to military exercises, new command structures, and a broader Western buildup in the High North.
Russia, however, wants the Arctic to remain “an area of peace and cooperation” and is ready to work with countries willing to engage on equal terms, Lavrov said.
Many of these countries were represented in Bishkek this week at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, where the focus was less on sanctions and confrontation than on cooperation, connectivity, and a changing global order.
Putin joined Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and other leaders from across Eurasia to discuss future development opportunities.
Putin told the summit that the emergence of a new multipolar world order is “irreversible” and called for countries of the Global South and East to receive greater representation in global institutions.
Another American strike, another civilian target
In the Middle East, however, diplomacy appears to have failed once again as the US resumed attacks on Iran on Tuesday. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks against US military facilities across the region.
Despite claiming to only target Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps sites near the Strait of Hormuz, one US weapon ended up striking a residential building in the southern Iranian town of Kuhestak where a wedding was being held.
The attack killed five people and wounded nearly 70 others. The dead reportedly included a 4-year-old and 16-year-old.
The incident has reignited accusations of war crimes against Washington, which has also been accused of attacking an elementary school in Minab on the first day of the war, killing around 170 people, most of them children.
In other news
One of the week’s more alarming numbers came not from a battlefield, but from a farm. A new study published in the Frontiers in Public Health journal estimated that as many as 433 million agricultural workers suffer acute pesticide poisoning every year – around 46% of all farmers worldwide.
This week, Russia also marked the anniversary of victory over Imperial Japan, and newly declassified Soviet records show the details of a massacre in Hailar, Manchuria, where Japanese forces executed 43 prisoners on August 9, 1945 – the day the Soviet offensive against the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo began.
RT also revisited the horror of Unit 731, the Japanese biological-warfare complex near Harbin where prisoners were infected with plague and cholera, subjected to frostbite and chemical-weapons experiments, and dissected alive.
Thousands died inside the facilities, while biological weapons developed there killed far more people across China. Check out the full deep-dive into the horrific history of the unit here.
What to watch out for
Germany could deliver another headache for Chancellor Friedrich Merz this weekend. Voters in Saxony-Anhalt go to the polls on Sunday, with the AfD polling around 41-42% against 22-23% for the CDU. An outright majority looks unlikely, but a landslide first-place finish would still be a major blow to the political establishment.
India then takes center stage. The first INNOPROM India fair opens in New Delhi on Wednesday, ahead of the BRICS summit on September 12-13. Modi said he expects Putin in India, with trade, Russia-India ties, and the broader multipolar agenda likely to dominate.
September 10 will also mark one year since the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, a killing that became a rallying point for Republicans and sharpened the debate over political violence in the US.

articles.title: Fresh US Fighter Jets Rotate into Middle East as Trump Tries to Up Pressure on Iran
articles.body:
The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended pressure campaign against Iran.
The move will free up units that have been based in the region far beyond the Air Force’s usual six-month deployments. More fighter unit rotations are expected in the coming weeks.
Units on their way home include the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard, which flies F-35 Lightning II aircraft. F-16 Fighting Falcons from the 555th Fighter Squadron based at Aviano Air Base, Italy, are also returning, according to people familiar with the matter and data collected by the open-source research group the Military Air Tracking Alliance.
The departing units have been deployed overseas since last year. The Vermont F-35s first deployed to Puerto Rico in December 2025 and supported the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, before deploying to the Middle East ahead of the U.S. air war against Iran. The Vermont ANG’s F-35s were spotted transiting through RAF Lakenheath, U.K., on their way back home. The F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since November.
Arriving in CENTCOM are F-16s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing. Twelve F-16s from the Ohio ANG departed Lajes in the Azores on Sept. 4, according to local aircraft spotters. The planes, which arrived on the Portuguese island on Aug. 29, are due to head to the Middle East.
Other units likely to deploy in the coming weeks include the 115th Fighter Wing of Wisconsin Air National Guard, which flies F-35s, sources said.
A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not respond to a request for comment.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month that the U.S. is stepping up its economic sanctions campaign to try to stop Iran from interfering with oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz while pressing Tehran to make concessions on its nuclear program. That is in addition to the ongoing American maritime blockade.
“If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart,” Bessent told CNBC last month.
But U.S. officials also say that the increased economic pressure might lead Iran to retaliate militarily. Fighting in the region flared up late last month when the U.S. struck Iranian launchers that were preparing to launch rockets with mines into the strait, and Iran retaliated by firing ballistic missiles at American forces in Jordan.
The new U.S. pressure campaign is likely to reduce the need for defensive and offensive munitions in the near term. But it still requires an ongoing military presence in the region and efforts to manage operational demands on the force.
The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand earlier this week after spending nine months at sea. The Lincoln took part in Operation Epic Fury—which officially lasted from Feb. 28 to early April—and then helped enforce a U.S. military blockade of Iranian ports and partook in tit-for-tat clashes against the Iranians for months.
Dozens of Air Force and Navy fighter jets remain deployed to the Middle East.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and 167 drones - how many were shot down and where there were hits
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and 167 drones - how many were shot down and where there were hits
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones; 128 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed. The Russian strikes resulted in fatalities.
On the night of September 5, Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones at Ukraine, up to half of them jet-powered. 128 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed. Missiles and drones hit their targets, but some did not reach them. UNN reports this citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Updated as of 9:35
What was used to attack and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, on the night of September 5 (starting at 6:00 p.m. on September 4), the enemy attacked with Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh regions, as well as 167 Shahed-type attack UAVs (about half of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were shot down
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:30 a.m., air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 128 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 23 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 1 location. In addition, some enemy weapons did not reach their targets; information about them is being clarified
The attack is ongoing; enemy UAVs are in the airspace.
Where there were hits
Kyiv region. According to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service on September 5, the Russians once again launched a massive attack on Kyiv region, injuring 2 people. The consequences were recorded in three districts:
-  in Bucha district, a warehouse caught fire. During firefighting operations, the enemy launched a follow-up strike on a nearby warehouse building; 
-  in Boryspil, a hit caused a fire and partially destroyed a nine-story residential building. The roof caught fire, and structures on the ninth floor were destroyed. 2 people were injured, and rescuers evacuated 15 residents. Psychologists from the State Emergency Service provided people with the necessary assistance; 
-  in Obukhiv district, rescuers extinguished fires in ecosystems caused by falling debris from Russian unmanned aerial vehicles. 
The response to the consequences of the attack is ongoing.
Dnipropetrovsk region. 4 people were killed and another 6 injured as a result of Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk region, the State Emergency Service reported on September 5. The consequences were recorded in four districts:
-  in Kamianske district, the Russians attacked an industrial enterprise. 4 people were killed and another 5 injured; 
-  in Nikopol district, a 62-year-old man was injured. Private homes and an apartment building were damaged; 
-  Synelnykove and Pavlohrad districts were also struck - an enterprise was damaged.  
Rescuers extinguished all fires caused by the shelling.
Mykolaiv. As the State Emergency Service noted on September 5, 2 people were injured in Mykolaiv as a result of Russian attacks. On September 4 and during the night of September 5, Russian forces repeatedly attacked one of the city’s shopping centers with drones. According to reports on social media, this was preliminarily the "Epicentr" shopping center.
According to the State Emergency Service, the hits damaged the shopping areas and caused fires. Those injured included a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl.
Rescuers worked under the constant threat of repeated strikes. Because of the danger, personnel were withdrawn to a safe distance several times. As soon as the situation allowed, rescuers returned to dealing with the aftermath of the attack. This was once again a civilian infrastructure facility - a place where ordinary people had come just yesterday, the State Emergency Service emphasized.
Zaporizhzhia. Explosions were heard in Zaporizhzhia region from the morning of September 5. Ivan Fedorov, the former head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, reported that the enemy was attacking Zaporizhzhia, with fires breaking out in various districts of the city. A private house was destroyed. Russian unmanned aerial vehicles struck a parking lot and non-residential buildings. No information about casualties had been received so far.
Sumy. According to Serhii Kryvosheienko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration, on September 5, the enemy continues to strike infrastructure facilities in the city. Almost at midnight, an FPV drone strike via fiber-optic connection was recorded at one of the shopping centers. The strike caused a fire, which was promptly extinguished. There were no casualties. Information about the consequences is being clarified.
Odesa region. Oleg Kiper, head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration, said on September 5 that during the night the enemy again struck warehouses containing goods that had been attacked earlier. The strikes caused a fire at a warehouse used to store food products. Fortunately, there were no fatalities or casualties. The fire has now been extinguished.
The State Emergency Service showed the aftermath of the Russian attack in Odesa region.
An air-raid alert was also heard in other regions during the night of September 5, reaching as far as the western regions of Ukraine. In particular, in Rivne region.

articles.title: Putin refused to make concessions regarding Ukraine after the CIA chief's visit - WP
articles.body:
Putin refused to make concessions regarding Ukraine after the CIA chief's visit - WP
Kyiv • UNN
Ratcliffe failed to convince Putin to make concessions regarding Ukraine. After the visit, Russia intensified its strikes on civilian infrastructure.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe failed to persuade Russian dictator vladimir putin to make concessions regarding Ukraine during his recent visit to moscow. putin may instead be preparing for a further escalation of the war. The Washington Post reports this, citing sources, and UNN relays.
Details
"vladimir putin, seeking to take advantage of Ukraine's severely weakened air defense system, is intensifying a bombing campaign that he believes will force Kyiv to concede on some of its key territorial demands, possibly as early as this winter," the publication writes.
It is noted that in the 10 days since the rare and unexpected visit to moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Russian forces have intensified missile strikes and attacks by jet-powered drones, targeting civilian infrastructure, including energy and water-supply facilities, supermarkets, and food warehouses.
Against the backdrop of the worsening state of the Russian economy and growing public discontent, putin expressed confidence this week in the successful course of the war.
His words, the publication writes, appear to confirm assessments that Ratcliffe's visit not only failed to persuade the head of the kremlin to end the war but may also have strengthened his determination to avoid a ceasefire and continue pressuring Ukraine to cede territory to moscow.
In moscow, Ratcliffe warned his counterparts in the Russian security services that escalating the war would have the opposite effect. According to three people familiar with the course of his talks, he urged a return to negotiations, arguing that russia's position was weak and would continue to deteriorate.
However, after the meetings, Ratcliffe felt that he had delivered the intended message, "but was unable to change the situation." russia perceived the visit as an "attempt to persuade putin to stop, but putin interpreted it as weakness."
"The message was: things are not going very well for you. It is time to talk. Let's sort this out, because in six months or a year things will be even worse for you," the source said.
putin's response to the visit, the publication indicates, appears to have consisted of continuous, round-the-clock airstrikes on Ukraine, as well as his statements at a regional security conference in Kyrgyzstan, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and promised support to Tehran in its war with the United States.
"The escalation of Russian strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities following Ratcliffe's visit may be a certain signal to Washington that russia is continuing its offensive operation and that there is no need to change its position and become more flexible," the source said.
Russia's military advance in Ukraine has virtually stalled, while its budget is becoming increasingly strained: the deficit had grown to $74.4 billion by the end of July, or 2.8% of GDP, significantly exceeding the government's initial forecast of 1.6% for this year.
The advance of Russian troops toward the administrative borders of Donetsk region, a strategically important area of the fortress belt in eastern Ukraine, has been stalling for several months. But the recent rise in oil prices, caused by the resumption of hostilities between Iran and the United States, emboldened putin, the publication writes.
This allowed the Russian leadership to believe that it could still achieve gains regarding Ukraine, even though the chief economist of one of russia's largest state-owned banks publicly warned that russia cannot win a war of attrition against Ukraine as long as Kyiv is supported by the West, a Moscow businessman said.
"There is a view in the kremlin that a few more months of war are not a problem for russia and the Russian economy, but for Ukraine it is a huge problem," the Russian businessman said.

articles.title: Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks: Report
articles.body:
Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks
About 50 officers on the US Joint Staff have been interrogated over reports detailing depleted weapons stockpiles during Iran conflict, says The New York Times.
United States investigators have subjected about 50 members of the US military’s Joint Staff to lie detector tests following a series of unauthorised media leaks, according to a report by The New York Times (NYT).
The inquiry focused on whether civilian and military personnel leaked classified details to reporters, particularly concerning dwindling US ammunition reserves, the newspaper reported on Friday.

- list 2 of 3US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
- list 3 of 3At least five killed in Sudan’s South Kordofan in attack by rebel group
The polygraph examinations took place last month after news outlets published several reports highlighting severe drops in key weapons supplies, including long-range missiles and Patriot air defence interceptors. US officials had pushed back on these reports, insisting their weapons stockpiles were more than sufficient.
In a statement to the NYT, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to address internal administrative or investigative actions directly, but emphasised that the department takes leaks of national security information “extremely seriously and investigates accordingly”.
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added.
The Joint Staff, which consists of between 1,500 and 2,000 military and civilian staff, plays a key role in coordinating operational strategy, policy and war planning with combat commands globally.
Unprecedented move
Sources familiar with the inquiry told the NYT that the aggressive push was designed not only to identify the individuals behind the disclosures, but also to deter potential future leakers.
Legal and military experts say the scale of the investigation is unprecedented, as the top ranks of the US armed forces have never undergone widespread polygraph testing in modern history.
The move follows widespread reporting on how active military operations involving Iran have severely strained US weapon reserves, causing internal debates over the broader direction of the conflict.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pushed officials to crack down on unauthorised disclosures. In addition to calling for strict enforcement, Trump has publicly branded critical media coverage regarding munition shortages and the administration’s handling of the conflict in Iran as “treasonous”.
The persistent leaks have deepened an atmosphere of deep distrust inside the Pentagon, which current and former officials attribute to the management style of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Operating alongside a tight circle of close aides, Hegseth has ousted or blocked the promotions of at least 80 generals, admirals and senior officials during his tenure, the report said.
The Pentagon has launched multiple leak probes in response to media coverage of Hegseth’s leadership, even as he faced criticism for sharing sensitive operational details in a Signal group chat.
The internal tensions escalated further last month when the Defence Department fired the top editor and publisher of Stars and Stripes, an independent, government-funded military news publication.
Staff members said the move was direct retaliation for stories detailing deteriorating conditions on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln.
Despite the mounting friction, Trump has backed Hegseth, publicly praising his performance as “fantastic”.

articles.title: Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran
articles.body:
The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.
Back in July, the Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit announced plans to develop a low-cost drone to do all the missions that an MQ-9 can do today, and when necessary fly in groups to overwhelm an enemy’s anti-drone capabilities and force them to expend large numbers of munitions. They called the effort Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA.
At the time, officials said they wanted to have a prototype to test fly within 21 months of a contract, and then 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031 to achieve initial operating capability.
Now, though, officials are targeting a more ambitious timeline. During a media roundtable at the Pentagon, DIU military deputy Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel said the MMA program will try to follow DIU’s typical timeframe of prototyping a system within a year of a contract, and then fielding it at scale within three years—as soon as 2029.
Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said those goals changed “fairly recently,” when Air Force Secretary Troy Meink “called us in and said ‘You need to move faster.’”
That urgency, Niemi acknowledged, came at least partly in response to the significant losses the MQ-9 fleet has taken in the past year or so during operations against Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Since the start of the Iran war, the Air Force has lost at least 45 MQ-9s, roughly a quarter of its fleet. The service was already thinking about what it needed to succeed the MQ-9 as a medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platform, but Niemi said the combat losses pushed it to move faster.
“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” Niemi said.
Replacing, Not Reinventing, the MQ-9
The MQ-9 has long been a workhorse of the Air Force fleet, valued by combatant commanders for its long endurance, loitering ability, and ability to combine strike and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach called the Reaper the “most valuable player” of Operation Epic Fury in a May congressional hearing.
Unsurprisingly, then, officials said they were eager to replace the ones lost in combat. Niemi said the Air Force has “spent a lot of time and energy” in recent months trying to figure out how to do so and found “there’s not a lot of good options to immediately replace those aircraft.”
The Air Force considered General Atomics’ MQ-9B, a larger and more complex—and more expensive—version of the MQ-9A, Niemi said. Ultimately, officials concluded the MQ-9B was not the right choice because the Air Force needed something more “attritable,” or inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.
“If you don’t like losing an MQ-9A that cost on the order of $50 million, with the sensors, you’re probably not going to like losing an MQ-9B at a higher price point,” Niemi said.
For that reason, the Air Force decided to go all-in on the MMA concept. The Air Force plans to field at least 180 of the drones, Niemi said, but probably more than that.
In order to move fast and keep costs down, Niemi said the Air Force plans to “accept prudent risk” on the MMA program. Kunkel also said the Air Force wants “significantly increased levels of competition” to keep costs down.
As the Air Force wrote out what attributes MMA drones would need, Niemi added, it tried to allow as much flexibility as possible and not include hyper-specific requirements that “push technology to the very edge.”
“When that happens, you’re going to pay a lot for it, because it’s hard to do,” Niemi said. “It takes a lot of engineering, cutting-edge science, emergent technologies, things like that. So we’re trying to be more aligned with sort of an ‘80 percent is good enough,’ [using] mature technologies” approach.
That means MMA won’t have the latest and greatest flight control systems, engines, or manufacturing processes, he said—and they’ll actually resemble the MQ-9 in some key ways: they’ll likely have long-aspect wings and will likely be powered by turboprop engines.
One way officials are looking to differ from the MQ-9, though, are higher levels of autonomy and automation than the MQ-9A has today, Niemi said—“more mouse clicks and keyboard strokes instead of a stick and throttle.” That will reduce the number of Airmen needed to operate MMA drones and allow a single Airman to operate multiple drones simultaneously.
At the same time, Niemi said MMAs won’t have the same level of autonomy as the Air Force’s flagship autonomous drone program, Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
“It’s not going out and autonomously finding targets and employing weapons,” Niemi said of the MMA drone. “It’s more like a truck that’s carrying packages, whether it’s a sensor package or whether it’s a weapon, to a point where it can be employed.”
CCAs and MMAs
While CCAs and MMAs will both be unmanned and have some kind of autonomy software, Niemi was quick to note there will be major differences between the two.
“They’re going to look very different,” Niemi said. The MMA is “going to look like an MQ-9, and [CCA is] going to look more like a fighter, like you’ve seen in the current too CCAs that we’re flying.”
The Air Force wants MMA drones to be able to fly about 4,000 miles—more than twice the expected range of autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft drones—and carry a heavy payload, although they will be slower than CCAs, Niemi said.
Those differences extend to price, too—while the Air Force is targeting $10 million for an MMA drone, it’s hoping for $20 million per CCA once they reach full production. Those costs are for just the base aircraft, excluding sensors, weapons or other equipment that might be loaded onto them.
From an acquisition perspective, the Air Force is hoping to use the same methods across the CCA and MMA programs to keep costs down and production simple.
That includes moving quickly to award contracts and keeping several vendors on contract to provide a variety of drones. Like CCAs, MMA drones will also use open architecture, Niemi said. That will ensure the drones have standardized interfaces and could be easily upgraded with newer sensor packages or weapons capabilities, even from different vendors, he said. This would also allow MMAs to be tailored with the gear needed for a particular mission.
“If you want to build a package that’s going to go on this new aircraft, as long as it conforms to this [standardized interface], we can do it very speedily and very readily,” Niemi said. “That’s something we struggle with at the opposite end of the spectrum, something like the F-35, where it’s very very hard to incorporate new things onto it, because of the construct and the architecture of that system.”
The Air Force also wants manufacturers to be able to produce MMA drones in large numbers, Niemi said, but also be able to ramp production up or down as needed, such as if the Air Force started losing large numbers in a heated conflict. Keeping MMAs simple is the best way to ensure that production flexibility, he said.
“If you wanted to suddenly ramp up production of something like an F-35, it’s not a limiting factor so much as money, as the ability to build out your production capacity and actually crank more of those things out,” Niemi said. “And the more complex the aircraft, the harder that problem is. … In major combat operations, depending on who you’re fighting, we could be losing dozens [of MMA drones] a day, and so you have to figure out how do you adjust the industrial capacity in order to make [necessary production levels] happen.”
General Atomics, which also makes the MQ-9, is planning to pitch a newly designed drone it calls Wildfire for the MMA program.
“Our new Wildfire aircraft addresses all of the concerns posed by the MMA solicitation,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement to reporters. “We can deliver years earlier and maintain the same high quality. You can have everything that makes Reaper special, plus more, at a price that doesn’t break the bank.”

articles.title: Combat Continues as Russia Rejects Ceasefire
articles.body:
The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) announced on Saturday, Sept. 5, that combat operations are ongoing following Russia’s refusal to agree to a proposed mutual ceasefire between Sept. 5 and Sept. 9.
The General Staff of the AFU told Ukrainska Pravda and Suspilne that a unilateral ceasefire is impossible because it would endanger military personnel, adding that defensive tasks are being executed in full according to plan.

Dmytro Filatov, commander of the 1st Separate Assault Regiment, stated that while the General Staff issued orders restricting strikes at an operational depth, no limitations were imposed on tactical-level combat.
The Russian Ministry of Defense confirmed its refusal to observe a temporary truce, publishing a report on Saturday detailing its overnight combined strikes on industrial facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region and logistics and energy infrastructure in the Mykolaiv and Odesa regions.
Overnight strikes and proposed diplomatic pause
The Russian Defense Ministry’s claims correspond with reported strikes across southern and central Ukraine early Saturday.
A Russian ballistic missile struck an industrial enterprise in Kamianske in the Dnipropetrovsk region, killing four people and injuring five others. Regional authorities reported that three individuals were hospitalized, including a 30-year-old woman requiring intensive care.
In Mykolaiv, consecutive jet-powered “Shahed” drone strikes hit an Epicenter shopping center late Friday and early Saturday, injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl and triggering a large fire.
The Skeleton Putin Needs
The Saturday attacks follow a Friday strike that damaged a nine-story residential building in Boryspil, Kyiv region, where a fire broke out on the roof and in an upper-floor apartment.
The sustained aerial campaign comes despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Friday announcement proposing a mutual halt to airstrikes.
The proposal was intended to accommodate the upcoming diplomatic mission of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are scheduled to visit Moscow and Kyiv this weekend.
