articles.title: Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
articles.body:
Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
As oil tanker struck off Kharg island, Trump threatens one of the remaining parts of Iran’s nuclear complex.
United States President Donald Trump says Washington may strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain “very soon”, in just the latest in a series of threats he has made against the heavily fortified underground site located next to the bombed-out Natanz enrichment complex.
Just hours after he made that threat, an Iranian oil tanker off Kharg Island was struck by four US missiles, according to Iranian news outlet Khabar Fouri. Kharg Island is the main hub for Iran’s oil exports, handling about 90 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran war: Why US midterms could be a pivotal moment
- list 2 of 4South Korea mulls ‘contributions’ in Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 4 of 4US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
Trump made the threat against Pickaxe Mountain as he was speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, saying the US knows “everybody that’s moving at Pickaxe” and across Iran.
His remarks echoed a similar threat he made back in mid-July, when he stated on the Hugh Hewitt Show: “We’re going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready … We’ll probably give Pickaxe a shot relatively soon.”
The latest threat comes more than six months into the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28, amid mixed messages about the war from the Trump administration.
On Friday, Trump sought to downplay the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes”, while a day earlier, at a White House news briefing, Vice President JD Vance appeared to suggest the conflict had cooled and to shrug off an alleged US strike on a wedding in southern Iran with “sometimes things happen“.
At a White House briefing this week, Vance said of the conflict with Iran that he “wouldn’t call it a war” and claimed there was “no active shooting right now”.
But the US and Iran have exchanged attacks this week, including a US hit close to Iran’s oil infrastructure on Kharg Island.
Meanwhile, talks related to Iran’s nuclear programme have remained in limbo since a 60-day negotiating window expired in mid-August without a deal.
Iran says it is not undertaking any work at the Natanz nuclear site.
Its Khatam al-Anbiya central military headquarters has warned that bombing the nearby mountain would amount to a renewal of war across the region, at a time when the Trump administration would prefer to keep the war contained before pivotal mid-term elections.
So why has Pickaxe Mountain become the latest focus of Trump’s threats – again?
What is Pickaxe Mountain?
Known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, the site sits roughly 220km (140 miles) south of the capital Tehran, in Isfahan province, and just 2km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz enrichment plant.
US intelligence reports indicate that the facility has been excavated deep inside the mountain, beneath hundreds of metres of solid granite rock, to protect it from powerful bombs designed to penetrate bunkers.
The main chambers are thought to lie at least 100 metres (330ft) underground.
Some Western analysts have speculated that the mountain was intended to house an undeclared enrichment plant, a hedge against attacks on Iran’s known facilities.
The Institute for Science and International Security, which tracks the site by satellite, has assessed that it is still under construction and not yet operational.
However, Iran has always maintained that it is developing a nuclear power programme only, and does not have plans to build a nuclear weapon.
Why does Pickaxe Mountain matter?
Because it is intact.
Pickaxe Mountain was left alone during the US’s June 2025 strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at the end of the 12-day Israel war on Iran, and has escaped the current war almost entirely; the Institute for Science and International Security has recorded only the destruction of a vehicle on a nearby spoil pile.
With Iran’s centrifuge manufacturing base and enrichment halls at other sites damaged in the war, analysts see the tunnels as the most obvious place for Tehran to rebuild: For component production, assembly or enrichment of uranium.
The Wall Street Journal reported in July that Israel had passed Washington intelligence suggesting thousands of centrifuges had been moved inside the facility late last year, a claim the US has not confirmed.
Trump has been less alarmist than Israel.
Centrifuges only matter if there is uranium to put through them; the machines concentrate uranium gas, and without a supply of it they cannot produce anything.
How much damage has been done to Iran’s nuclear sites?
According to most estimates, a considerable amount.
The European Council on Foreign Relations estimates that the 2025 strikes likely destroyed many of the roughly 18,000 centrifuges then operating at Iran’s Natanz and Fordow facilities, along with several centrifuge production sites and Ardakan, Iran’s only yellowcake milling plant. Yellowcake is powdered uranium concentrate obtained from milled uranium ore.
Nearly 4,000 additional centrifuges were installed but idle at the time; however, they may have survived the strikes.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed further damage to the entrance buildings of Natanz’s underground enrichment plant in March 2026, although it detected no additional impact on the plant itself.
The Institute for Science and International Security reported in June that tunnel entrances at all three main sites remain sealed, that there is no evidence of any enrichment taking place, and that the centrifuge programme still appears to have been destroyed.
Didn’t Trump say Iran’s nuclear sites had already been destroyed?
Yes. After the June 2025 attacks, Trump said the three sites had been “completely and totally obliterated”.
However, just days later, a leaked preliminary US Defence Intelligence Agency assessment concluded that the sites had been significantly damaged but not destroyed, estimating that the strikes had set Iran’s nuclear programme back by less than six months.
The situation today remains unclear.
“No one really knows what the state of Iran’s nuclear programme is at this moment; there’s a lot of uncertainty and ambiguity about how much damage Iran has suffered as a result of these last two wars,” Nader Hashemi, a professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera.
Iran is currently believed to be holding about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent.
But having the material is only part of the equation, Hashemi said.
In order for Iran to produce a nuclear weapon, it would have to enrich that uranium up to 90 percent.
That would require access to its centrifuges, “of which we don’t know to what extent they may have been damaged”, he said.
No inspector has entered the bombed sites, and Trump’s framing has shifted from “obliteration” to a promise to hit any site where Iran is “even thinking about nuclear”.
What do we know about Iran’s nuclear programme?
Less than at any point in two decades.
Just before the US-Israel attacks on Iran in June 2025, the IAEA verified about 10 tonnes of enriched uranium in total, including the 440kg stockpile enriched to 60 percent.
In theory, this amount of enriched uranium – should it be enriched to 90 percent – is enough to produce more than 10 nuclear warheads, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told Al Jazeera in early March. It is unclear where this stock may be, however.
Iran suspended cooperation with the agency after the strikes, and the IAEA now says it has no way to report on the size, location or composition of that stockpile, though it believes much of the 60-percent material is bottled up in tunnels at Isfahan.
On Friday, Trump claimed again that the US had prevented Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, arguing that Washington’s intervention had protected Israel and the wider Middle East.
Tehran insists the programme is peaceful, and has dismissed Washington’s focus on Pickaxe Mountain as a manufactured pretext for attacking it.

articles.title: Russia’s jet drones fly at 700 km/h. Ukraine is meeting them with 1970s heat-seekers
articles.body:
- Russia is launching more jet-propelled Geran drones and Banderol missiles
- Speeding along as fast as 700 km/hr, these munitions are hard to intercept
- Ukraine's fighters are up to the task—but they are reaching for missiles designed in the 1970s
Russia is launching more of its best jet-propelled attack drones and miniature cruise missiles at Ukrainian ports, cities, warehouses, and power plants. The speedy Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 drones and Banderol missiles can zoom right past Ukraine's ground-based guns and slower interceptor drones, so the Ukrainian air force is deploying more supersonic fighters to chase down the Russian munitions.
But there's a problem. The Ukrainian jets are running short of the missiles that work best against them.
A deepening shortage of infrared-guided AIM-9 missiles and radar-guided AIM-120 missiles for the Ukrainian air force's ex-European Lockheed Martin F-16 fighters has been reported elsewhere. Less well known is what has been happening to the Soviet-era missiles carried by Ukraine's older Mikoyan MiG-29 fighters.
The F-16 is probably the most numerous Ukrainian fighter type, with around 50 in service. But the MiG-29 is a close second. Despite steep losses of MiG-29s in the 55 months since Russia widened its war on Ukraine, Ukrainian aviation brigades may still fly dozens of the classic Soviet-made fighters. MiG-29s are daily sights in the sky over the port of Odesa in southern Ukraine as the twin-engine fighters chase down Russian missiles and drones.
The MiG-29 can carry the full array of Soviet-style air-to-air missiles in the Ukrainian inventory including the infrared-guided R-60 and R-73 and the radar-guided R-27. But the missile of choice for intercepting the 500 km/hr Gerans and 700 km/hr Banderols is the more modern R-73. The $300,000 heat-seeking missile is maneuverable and accurate at the close ranges that are typical of fighter-on-drone engagements. Its one known weakness is cloud: a Ukrainian pilot said in 2022 that the R-73 tracks poorly through it, which is part of why pilots sometimes fall back on the cannon.
Ukraine went to war in 2022 with substantial stocks of R-73s and surely received additional copies from allies. While Ukrainian industry built some components for the 1980s-vintage missiles, they were and still are assembled in Russia—so the supply is finite. And the rate of expenditure rose sharply as Ukraine pushed the R-73 into roles it was never built for: onto ground-based launchers, after the 9M33 missiles for its Soviet Osa air defense systems ran short, and even onto some of its robotic boats.
Down to the 1970s stock
The sign of that pressure is the return of the R-60—a missile designed in the 1970s and considered obsolete when Russia widened the war. Last month an R-60 was visible in the wreckage following the crash of a Ukrainian MiG-29. And this week, video circulated of a MiG-29 downing a Banderol with one at extremely low altitude.
Ukraine's air force had enough R-73s in 2022 that nobody expected to see R-60s again. Continuous interception of Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type drones changed that, Militarnyi reported. Nor is this improvisation: since November 2025 Ukraine has been running a program to modernize the R-60, replacing analog seeker components with digital ones to sharpen its infrared sensitivity, and adapting it for ground launch. Ihor Fedirko of the Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry called it a temporary way to put otherwise unusable missiles to work.
It's not that the R-60 isn't suitable for downing a Geran or Banderol. It's that it's less suitable than an R-73. "I don't think Ukraine would be using R-60 missiles unless it had nothing else left," one close observer of the Ukrainian air force noted.
Ukraine’s F-16s are so short of Western missiles that pilots fall back on jet’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which risks killing civilians below
The only other alternative is for a fighter to use its gun. But that's risky, as the pilot must fly dangerously close to a drone or missile before opening fire; the resulting explosion could take out both the interceptee and the interceptor.
In the same way Russia is exhausting Ukraine's long-range surface-to-air missile batteries by firing more ballistic missiles than Ukrainian forces can intercept with their dwindling supply of Patriot missiles, Russia may also be exhausting Ukraine's fighters and their limited stocks of short-range air-to-air missiles.
As the Ukrainian missiles run out, more of the Russian missiles and drones get through—and strike their targets.
Trending Now
The problem is going to get worse before it gets better. Russian industry is ramping up production of both the jet-propelled Geran models and the Banderol, and jet output overtook piston output in August. The Russians launched a reported 1,500 jet Gerans in July and 2,500 in August. Interception rates for the fast drones specifically ran as low as 50% in July, though they may have ticked up to 60% or even 70%.
But that's still too low considering that Ukrainian air defenders usually shoot down 90% of slower propeller-driven Geran-1s and Geran-2s. "Nobody wants interception rates in the 60s/70s," explained Michael Bohnert, an analyst for the RAND think tank in California.
New models of faster interceptor drones, which several Ukrainian manufacturers are scrambling to deliver to front-line forces, may help restore the 90% kill rate for even the fastest Gerans. But "jet-interceptor output has been behind jet-drone output," Bohnert noted. So it's likely that, for a few months at least, the Russians will have the numerical edge, and the Ukrainians will have no choice but to continue sortieing F-16s and MiG-29s to reinforce ground-launched air defenses.
But what happens when the fighters run out of even their oldest missiles?

articles.title: ‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike
articles.body:
Seven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows.
A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery to Gaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed.
The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.
However, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza.
More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’s own internal data suggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians.
The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless).
He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.”
He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”
Mendel was referring to a general policy of haflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in which haflala is to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers.
He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas's attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.”
When the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries.
An IDF statement said the airstrikes were a result of an “erroneous assessment that Hamas military operatives were present in the vehicles, rather than from an intention to target the organisation’s personnel”.
The statement added that “this assessment was compounded by serious failures to comply with applicable orders and procedures”. However, it said: “Following an in-depth examination of the findings and in light of the standards applicable under criminal law, it was determined that, despite the aforementioned failures, the circumstances of the incident did not give rise to a reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence warranting the opening of a criminal investigation.”
The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”
Britain, Australia and Canada denounced the prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman.
Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian, Australian Zomi Frankcom, Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation.
Mendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.
However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target.
The IDF statement said its activity in the Gaza Strip was “regulated by a broad range of binding written orders and standing directives governing the use of force, the approval processes for strikes, strikes against sensitive sites, and other matters” and that these incorporated “the rules of the laws of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack”.
The statement said that “a person does not become a lawful target merely because they are in the vicinity of an armed individual, come into contact with them, or travel alongside them”.
The IDF said: “Carrying a weapon may be a relevant factor in such an assessment, but is not sufficient on its own without meeting the definitions described above. In particular, and in the context of the incident in question, security personnel hired to protect a humanitarian convoy from looting do not become lawful targets merely because they are armed.”
An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.”
Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes.
“If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas – anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.”
A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination.
“You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of civilian casualties, but not the subsequent missiles.
“You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said.
The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator.
“I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.”
Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia.
The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit.
The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.”
The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities.
The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations.
“I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.”
He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.”

articles.title: Lithuania to Launch Integrated AI Drone Defense System
articles.body:
The Lithuanian Ministry of National Defense announced a state contract for an integrated airspace surveillance and control system designed to unify data from various institutions into a single ecosystem, LRT reported.
Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas stated that the system, powered by artificial intelligence, will aggregate data from military sensors, radars, and other agencies in real time. The initiative aims to improve the identification of drones within Lithuanian airspace and facilitate timely public warnings.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The government plans to allocate approximately €5 million ($5.8 million) for the project’s implementation.
“At the national level, the unified system will strengthen the capabilities of state institutions to warn and respond to air threats,” Kaunas said. “At the same time, this state order strengthens the competencies of Lithuanian business in the field of air defense.”
The ministry outlined a three-stage implementation plan, with a pilot program expected to launch in early 2027.
By 2027, the system will integrate all connected sensors and air defense assets to generate a comprehensive picture of the airspace. Data regarding detected objects will be transmitted to regional authorities and operators of critical infrastructure.
By 2028, the system is scheduled to be integrated with data transmission platforms utilized by NATO allies.
EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance to Hold Inaugural Meeting in Brussels
The project aligns with a government implementation plan requiring Lithuania to establish an integrated air defense and surveillance system capable of detecting and neutralizing unmanned aerial vehicles by the third quarter of 2028.
Latvian drone incident and false flag warnings
The procurement announcement follows recent unauthorized drone activity in the region and warnings from Lithuanian officials regarding potential Russian hybrid operations.
On Aug. 14, fighter jets participating in NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission shot down an unidentified drone that had breached Latvian airspace.
Following the incident, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius stated that the possibility of the drone being part of a Russian “false flag” operation could not be ruled out, though he noted evidence would remain inconclusive until the aircraft was recovered and analyzed.
Sinkevičius’s comments mirrored earlier warnings from Defense Minister Kaunas, who stated in August that national intelligence services possessed information indicating Russia was considering provocations in the Baltic region.
Kaunas warned at the time that the Kremlin might utilize captured Ukrainian drones to strike critical infrastructure in the Baltic states, aiming to create the false impression of Ukrainian involvement and undermine Western support for Kyiv.

articles.title: From HQ to the zero line: Ukraine’s Hrafit system answers one important question on an ordinary phone in a trench and on the road
articles.body:
A Ukrainian soldier in a trench or in a vehicle can now get a short alert on their phone the moment a Russian FPV drone or glide bomb starts closing in. The system behind it, Hrafit (Graphite), pulls together data from nearly all available radio-technical intelligence and surveillance into a single picture, ArmyInform reported.
The threat no longer stops at a command post. The warning reaches the soldier at an observation point, the sector command, and the commander-in-chief at once. To use it in a position, a soldier needs only a protected smartphone and satellite internet, including Starlink, and on the ground, it comes down to one short push notification.
Hrafit answers one question: Is the sky clear?
In modern combat, a second's hesitation can be enough for an infantry soldier in a trench or a crew in a vehicle to be caught by an FPV drone or a guided glide bomb. Hrafit is the Ukrainian answer, moving situational awareness onto an ordinary phone.
Military programmers built it for Ukraine's Defense Forces to answer the one question that matters most in the field: is the sky clear? Militarnyi reported that the system is being supplied to the Armed Forces, the National Guard, the Security Service, and the Border Guard Service.
It tracks drones and glide bombs
Working in real time, Hrafit flags a wide range of incoming threats:
- FPV drones, both kamikaze and loitering types
- tactical quadcopters such as the DJI Mavic, which are often used to direct fire
- winged Russian drones like the Molniya and Privet
- guided glide bombs and other aerial munitions
Three versions run from HQ to the trench
Hrafit runs on Android, iOS, and the web, in three versions.
The full version, for analysts, commanders, and electronic warfare and air defense operators, adds reporting, filters, frequency-band analysis, and a global map of the fighting.
For instance, Hrafit Lite strips down the interface for troops on the zero line, showing only the local area, so nothing distracts from the fight.
A third module, Sova (Owl), is built for logistics crews, drivers, and medical evacuation: it runs during a drive, moves its monitoring sector across the map with the vehicle, and warns of danger along the way.
Soldiers can learn the system through an official online course in the Army+ app, which teaches them to operate and configure Hrafit and issues a completion certificate.

articles.title: US targets oil tanker off Iran's Kharg Island
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to our coverage of the Middle East.
Iranian media reported that an oil tanker had been hit near the country's major oil hub of Kharg Island, days after Washington renewed its war campaign against Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate by attacking assets across the Gulf.
The US military said Saturday it had struck and destroyed three oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps after the Iranian military organisation fired on American warships.
"Following Iran's failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask. American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo... in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement on X.
Saturday's attacks come after US President Donald Trump again threatened to attack Iran's Pickaxe Mountain "soon". It also follows an unprecedented sanctions campaign aimed at pressuring the Iranian economy.
Meanwhile, Israel continues to strike southern Lebanon, with local media reporting multiple strikes along the border areas overnight and into Saturday morning. At least three people were killed and more than 20 others injured in Israeli strikes on Friday, according to the country's health ministry.
In Yemen, the Houthi militant group has launched a large-scale offensive on positions controlled by the Saudi-backed government in the country's Taiz province, killing at least 129 people.
Ten people were killed when a fuel tanker exploded on a highway in western Iran as a result of a traffic accident, state media reported on Saturday.
The tanker, which was travelling on the Hamedan-Sanandaj Highway, was involved in an accident due to a technical fault in the braking system, the governor of Sanandaj said, according to state media.
A fire has since been contained, the governor said.
Six people were also injured in the incident, the governor said.
GHM: Israel's war kills 73,751 Palestinians since Oct 2023
Israel's ongoing genocidal war has killed over 73,651 Palestinians since October 2023, Gaza's Health Ministry announced on Saturday.
A further 174,575 have been wounded, with hospitals reporting 27 over the past 48 hours.
Gaza's hospitals received 17 bodies over the past 48 hours, including five who were killed recently and one who died from their injuries. Authorities recovered 11 more bodies from the rubble.
Gaza rescue teams recover remains of 55 Palestinians
Gaza's rescue teams on Saturday recovered the remains of 55 Palestinians from under the rubble of a home that was destroyed by an Israeli attack, almost three years later.
The attack, which happened on 19 November 2023, destroyed the Malka family home, where over 60 people sought shelter.
Fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the country's Houthi rebels killed more than 60 people on Saturday, including civilians, medical and military sources told AFP.
According to three Yemeni military sources, 26 government troops were killed during several hours of fighting in the country's southwest, while medical and military sources from the Iran-backed Houthis said 31 rebel fighters were killed.
One medical source in the government-held city of Taiz said a missile strike also killed six civilians travelling by bus and wounded seven others.
A government official blamed the strike on the bus, travelling between Taiz and the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government in Aden, on the Houthis.

American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo... in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement on X.
Lebanon on Saturday raised the toll in Israeli strikes on the country's south and east overnight to five killed.
Lebanon's health ministry reported five people killed, including an 18-year-old woman, and 32 others wounded, including several women and children, in Israeli strikes on several locations on Friday, particularly in the Nabatieh region.
Iran accuses the US of targeting a tanker near Kharg Island
Iran on Saturday accused the US of attacking an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. The US did not immediately comment, but a new strike would raise the risk of sparking a new round of Iranian attacks on US allies and interests in the region.
The Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting said Saturday that four US missiles struck a tanker about six miles (10 kilometres) from Kharg Island. It said the crew was being evacuated and there were no casualties.
The report did not provide evidence or include comment from Iranian officials. US Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
At least four civilians have been killed after a Houthi missile targeted the Heijah al-Abd road south of Taiz, according to Yemen’s government-affiliated Saba TV.
A further nine others were injured.
Huckabee: Israel 'has responsibility' to ensure safety
Huckabee said that the Israeli government has a responsibility to ensure the safety of Palestinians in the West Bank after a sharp rise in settler attacks.
"One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that that happens," Ambassador Mike Huckabee told reporters as he met Palestinian-Americans in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Huckabee: Israel not planning forced displacement from Gaza
The US ambassador to Israel on Saturday said that there was no plan underway to force Palestinians out of Gaza, after Israeli ministers laid out ideas on how to expel the war-battered territory's two million people.
"I can tell you categorially there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will," Ambassador Mike Huckabee told reporters as he visited Palestinian-Americans in the West Bank.
Israeli forces detain several Palestinians in West Bank
Israeli forces detained several Palestinians on Saturday in the occupied West Bank, Wafa reports.
Israeli forces detained farmers in the northern Yarza community, east of Tubas and prevented them from working, the Yarza Village Council Chairman Mukhlis Masaeed said.
UN nuclear agency members draft resolution reporting Iran
The United States, Britain, France and Germany have drafted a resolution for possible consideration by the Board of Governors of the UN nuclear watchdog that seeks to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations, diplomats say.
Under those obligations, part of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow inspectors from the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
The diplomatic move has been under consideration since June 2025, when the IAEA board found Iran officially in noncompliance with its nonproliferation obligations for the first time in 20 years — one day before the US and Israel launched attacks against Iran’s nuclear sites.
A possible referral of Iran to the UN Security Council shifts responsibility to a higher authority that can enact further legally binding measures, including sanctions or asset freezes.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee visits an occupied West Bank village that is home to thousands of Palestinian Americans, amid a rise in Israeli settler attacks.
Iranian media on Saturday reported several explosions near the country's major oil hub of Kharg Island in the Gulf, days after renewed fighting broke out with the United States.
Fars news agency said blasts were heard by its correspondent but that there was no smoke visible, while the SNN news agency claimed "an Iranian tanker was targeted by the US" near the island.
There was no immediate comment from US or Iranian officials.

articles.title: Russia Continues Missile and Drone Strikes on Ukraine Amid Reports of Possible Suspension of Ukrainian Attacks
articles.body:
On the night of September 5, Russian troops continued to strike Ukraine with missiles and drone-launched rockets, following a statement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky regarding a possible suspension of Ukrainian long-range strikes during the visit to Moscow by special envoys of U.S. President Trump.
This is evidenced by data from the Ukrainian Air Force and local authorities.
After midnight in the city of Boryspil of the Kyiv region a Russian drone struck the roof of a nine-story residential building.
The strike caused a fire and damage to the roof and to one of the apartments on the top floor.
Later, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, reported that two women were injured and hospitalized with various injuries.
The Russians also struck the city of Kamianske in the Dnipropetrovsk region with several ballistic missiles.
The Regional Military Administration reported that the target of the missile strikes was an industrial facility. By morning, it was reported that four people had been killed and five wounded as a result of this attack.
“Three of the victims are in the hospital. Among them is a 30-year-old woman who is in intensive care. Medical personnel are providing the wounded with all necessary care,” said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional administration.
On the evening of September 4, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that during the visits of U.S. President Donald Trump’s special representatives, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow and Kyiv, Ukraine would ensure the “normal functioning of Russian airspace.”
“And just as we did during previous diplomatic visits by the U.S. side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are looking out for them, not for Russia,” Zelensky said.
The president noted that while negotiations are underway and logistical issues related to the U.S. delegation’s visit are being resolved, Ukraine will not carry out airstrikes. At the same time, he said, Russia must reciprocally ensure a cessation of airstrikes during this period. Axios reported yesterday that visits by Trump’s special envoys will take place this weekend.
The Ukrainian Armed Forces have also been ordered to observe a ceasefire along the front lines from 12:00 a.m. on September 5 to 11:59 p.m. on September 8.

articles.body:

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement that a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer ship had "successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" and that no American personnel were hurt.

Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, said the message to the IRGC was "clear": "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours."
“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet," he added.
Iranian media outlets had earlier reported that an Iranian oil tanker had been struck by US forces near Kharg Island on Saturday morning, close to the Strait of Hormuz.
Multiple explosions were heard and the tanker was said to have been evacuated, with no casualties reported at the time, according to the same initial reports.
It comes a day after Tehran reportedly launched anti-ship missiles against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian media did not provide details as to the targets nor any damage inflicted in the alleged attacks.

CENTCOM said it had taken "limited, precise action" against IRGC minelaying forces, which it said had posed an "imminent threat" in the waterway.
The IRGC confirmed strikes had hit Larak Island and vowed to retaliate, later launching its own attacks on US bases across the Middle East.

articles.title: Qatar rejects Iran claim strikes only targeted US military sites
articles.body:
Qatar said on Friday that official records it submitted to the UN show Iranian missiles struck civilian, commercial and residential areas in the country, rejecting Tehran’s attempt to cite a Qatari document as evidence that its attacks were limited to US military facilities. 
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari made the remarks in a statement responding to a post on US social media company X by Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. 
Baghaei cited a safety and security risk assessment prepared by Qatar for the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference, claiming the document confirmed that Iranian strikes exclusively targeted US military facilities in Qatar and did not target civilian areas, except for gas facilities in Ras Laffan that he alleged were being used in US military operations against Iran. 
Qatar hosts the Al Udeid Air Base, which houses the Combined Air Operations Center responsible for command and control of air operations across the US military’s Central Command area of responsibility, as well as a forward headquarters for the command, according to US military information. 
“If the Iranian side wishes to reference official documentation, we invite it to refer to the record formally submitted by the State of Qatar to the United Nations, rather than selectively quoting a security risk assessment prepared for operational purposes,” Al-Ansari said. 
“Qatar’s identical letters dated 1 March 2026 (S/2026/110) documented the launch of Iranian missiles over civilian, commercial and residential areas, resulting in damage and injuries to 16 people. Qatar’s letter dated 20 July also documented further attacks that injured three people, including a child,” he added. 
The attacks came amid the war that erupted on Feb. 28, when the US and Israel launched large-scale military strikes against Iran, followed by Iranian attacks on Israel and countries across the region, including Qatar. 
On the same day, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, as well as subsequent Iranian attacks that he said violated the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Since the beginning of the war, Qatar has sent letters to the UN and the Security Council documenting Iranian attacks on its territory. 
“The document now being cited by the Iranian side is a safety and security risk assessment prepared for the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference. It is neither a comprehensive factual record nor a legal assessment of the events,” said Al-Ansari. 
“In fact, it expressly acknowledges direct attacks inside the State of Qatar, including the 18 March attack on gas facilities in Ras Laffan, and refers to the temporary closure of Qatari airspace and the impact on civilian life. Selectively extracting a sentence from that document while disregarding its broader context is therefore misleading.”  
Al-Ansari said the success of Qatar Armed Forces in intercepting Iranian missiles and drones “does not diminish the gravity of these attacks, nor does it absolve those responsible of accountability.” 
“It is regrettable that the attack on Ras Laffan has been described as ‘alleged,’ despite having been formally documented in Qatar’s letter S/2026/207, particularly given that these facilities are national assets belonging to the Qatari people and form an integral part of the global energy security architecture,” he said. 
In the letter, Qatar told the Security Council that Iran launched seven ballistic missiles toward Ras Laffan Industrial City on March 18, with Qatari forces intercepting six while one missile struck the city, causing fires and significant damage. The area came under another missile attack in the early hours of the following day. 
Qatar said in the note that it had “distanced itself from this war from its outset” and sought to avoid becoming involved in the escalation, accusing Iran of continuing to target Qatari territory and neighboring countries. 
“The State of Qatar is not a party to this conflict. Attacks on its territory and civilian infrastructure, the endangerment of its population, and destabilizing actions in the Strait of Hormuz cannot be justified as ‘legitimate responses,’” said Al-Ansari. “Such acts constitute clear violations of international law, and no selective quotation or interpretation can alter that fact.” 
The exchange between Qatar and Iran comes amid renewed escalation between Washington and Tehran, with the two trading military strikes in early September in one of the fiercest rounds of escalation since July, while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues to be affected. 
“Guided by its longstanding position that dialogue and peaceful means remain the best path to resolving differences, Qatar will continue its diplomatic efforts and sustained endeavors to de-escalate tensions and promote security and stability in the region,” the Qatari spokesman said. 
Letters to UN, Security Council rep. 
In the letters sent to Guterres and France’s UN representative Jerome Bonnafont, who is holding the rotating presidency of the Security Council, Qatar rejected Iranian claims regarding recent territorial attacks, asserting its right to self-defense and compensation.
 The letters said Iranian claims cannot provide a legal basis for “unjustified and unlawful” attacks against Qatar. Doha argued that the strikes violate international law and UN Charter Article 2(4), which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. Qatar also cited UN Security Council Resolution 2817, which previously condemned the attacks as threats to international peace. 
Doha also dismissed Iran's invocation of Article 51 self-defense and pointed out that Tehran's reliance on the 1974 UN General Assembly definition of aggression actually undermines its own position. The letters noted that the definition explicitly considers the bombardment of another state's territory and the blockade of ports, referencing Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, as acts of aggression. 
Qatar accused Tehran of targeting critical civilian infrastructure, including energy facilities, oil tankers, and commercial vessels in violation of the Geneva Conventions.

articles.title: Ukraine says 4 killed, 7 injured in Russian overnight strikes
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Four people were killed and seven others injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine, Ukrainian officials said Saturday.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russia struck an industrial enterprise in Kamianske, killing four people and injuring five others, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram.
In the Kyiv region, two people were injured in an attack on Boryspil, Governor Timur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
Tkachenko said efforts were underway to assess and address the consequences of the strike on a nine-story residential building.
The Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram that 128 Russian drones were shot down overnight.
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said that its forces struck two of Ukraine's largest suppliers of metal products for the military in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
The ministry said Russian forces also struck logistics centers, a dry cargo ship, two fuel storage and distribution facilities and an electronic intelligence center in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Kyiv regions.
It also said Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 53 Ukrainian drones across Russia, annexed Crimea and over the Black Sea.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Kyiv “will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace” during an expected visit to Moscow by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“We are looking out for them, not for Russia,” Zelenskyy wrote on US social media platform X.
“There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit,” he added.
 
Axios news website and Russian state news agency Tass reported, citing sources, that the two US envoys will visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy accuses Russia of 'demonstrative strikes' on Kiev airports amid US envoys' visit
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday accused Russia of carrying out “demonstrative strikes” on airports in Kiev and Boryspil overnight ahead of a planned visit to the Ukrainian capital by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kiev Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy wrote on the US social media platform X.
He said Moscow had deliberately targeted the airports “for the first time in a while”.
“Russian-Iranian ‘shaheds’ in response to American diplomacy,” he said.
“We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.”
Zelenskyy said Kiev would not allow threats to undermine diplomacy on its part, stressing that Ukraine was interested in bringing peace closer.
“Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” he added.
Witkoff, Kushner in Moscow
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday for talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
According to the agency, a special jet carrying the two US envoys landed at Vnukovo Airport.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev arrived at the airport to meet the American representatives, the agency reported.
Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner would visit Kiev on Sunday following their trip to Moscow.
Neither envoy has previously visited Kiev, although both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began.
Their latest visit was on January 22, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.
Meanwhile, five people were killed and five others wounded in Ukrainian strikes over the past 24 hours in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's Luhansk region, Leonid Pasechnik, the Russian governor, said on Saturday.

articles.title: Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say
articles.body:
Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia, Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week.
The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war with Europe, weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict.
The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe.
Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiring Nato to focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict.
One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat.
They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted.
The private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience.
A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may be losing the so-called hybrid war with Russia, and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy.
Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict.
The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month.
One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as a Belarusian citizen with a Russian passport who appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa.
The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning.
Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD in Germany, on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”.
One proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline.
The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US.
“Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. These are really huge and existential challenges requiring greater integration in defence,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the chair of the MSC.
He argued the E5 grouping offers a way of including all the European countries with substantial defence industrial capacity and may later be able to incorporate Ukraine in the context of a truce since Kyiv now has the largest and strongest army in Europe.
Advocates of the E5 insist it will neither duplicate nor underline Nato, but fears were expressed that the US would nevertheless block a stronger European pillar inside Nato. “The US are better at talking about burden shifting than power sharing,” said one diplomat.
Italy is one of the E5 states most concerned about the impact of Russia’s hybrid warfare on its domestic politics as Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing administration – which has governed more moderately than many expected, and cultivated a pro-Ukraine image abroad – becomes its longest-running since the second world war.
The Italian foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, warned Italy was suffering daily cyber-attacks, adding it was not immune from potential Russian interference in next year’s national elections, the first time an Italian politicians has warned the election may be manipulated.
“There are many ways to wage hybrid warfare, it is not done using bombs, planes or tanks,” the minister said.
Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, one of Meloni’s closest political allies, has said it was stupid not to recognise the level of Russian interference.
He warned this summer at the Nato summit in Ankara: “We don’t have the antibodies and we’re penetrable: analyse bots and you’ll see it. The increase occurred thanks to social media.”
His doubts have grown given Moscow’s ability to operate across so many domains, including social media, AI, cybersecurity, databases and critical infrastructure. On Tuesday, he said the Russian threat was growing all the time.
Crosetto also said he recognises Russia is exploiting real problems such as low wages, and so attributing government unpopularity to Russian disinformation risks misidentifying a malaise afflicting western societies, including a general weariness with the cost of the war in Ukraine,
In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the far-right Futuro Nazionale who has challenged the stability of Meloni’s coalition, is widely seen as the most probable carrier of the Russian message in the coming election, that could come as early as April.
Speaking before the investigation into whether his party represents a revival of fascism, Vannacci gloried in the criticism. “Just discovered that I am a ‘Manchurian candidate’ sent by the Russian federation to complain about the unaffordable petrol prices in my country Italy,” he said. “Forgive me, but I still find it hard to accept the idea that dissent from Brussels’ orthodoxy is now, in practical terms, tantamount to disloyalty towards the west.”
In an attempt to shift perceptions so Ukraine is seen not as a financial burden but rather as teaching Europe modern warfare, Crosetto has recruited the former Ukraine defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as his unpaid adviser for innovation. Ischinger praised the decision, describing Ukraine as possessing the best equipped and most modern army in Europe.
In Ukraine, 200,000 drones are being built each month, with the goal of producing more than 7m by 2026. To support this growth, 500 small and medium-sized companies have sprung up, assembling drones even in small workshops, using mostly Chinese components.

articles.title: SBU exposes Russian spy operating within Ukrainian Armed Forces in Kharkiv
articles.body:
SBU exposes Russian spy operating within Ukrainian Armed Forces in Kharkiv
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
One of those detained is a local man who was mobilized into a Ukrainian Territorial Defense brigade. He was working for Russian military intelligence, better known as the GRU, and was passing information to the enemy from "inside" the Ukrainian military.
The investigation established that Russian intelligence recruited the Kharkiv resident through his neighbor, a professor at a Kharkiv university whom the SBU exposed in March this year for adjusting Russian strikes on the city.
After the university lecturer was detained, the suspect, acting on orders from the enemy, joined the Ukrainian military, where he was assigned as a reserve soldier in a reserve company of a combat unit.
There, under the guise of official trips, the agent monitored the locations of Ukrainian air defense and electronic warfare units, as well as defensive fortifications around Kharkiv.
He also marked the locations of local combined heat and power plants and key electrical substations supplying the city and surrounding areas on Google Maps.
The suspect later recruited his unemployed wife to cooperate with the enemy. Initially, she walked around the city to identify locations where Ukrainian troops were based and passed the intelligence to her husband. She later reported directly to her Russian handler.
The man's next assignment was to undergo training as an unmanned systems operator and hand over to Russian intelligence materials obtained during the training.
After completing the courses, the serviceman hoped to receive a promotion to a position in a UAV unit, which would allow him to expand his espionage activities in favor of the aggressor state.
SBU officers exposed the agent couple, documented their criminal activities step by step and detained both suspects: the man during another intelligence-gathering mission and his wife at their place of residence.
During searches, investigators seized 12 smartphones, four laptops and two tablets, which the suspects regularly switched in order to maintain covert communications with the Russian GRU.
SBU investigators notified both detainees that they were suspected of violating Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.
The suspects are being held in custody without the right to bail. They face life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

articles.title: Air defense downs 128 of 167 Russian drones, impacts recorded at 23 locations

articles.title: Who really benefits from the CIA chief’s Moscow trip?
articles.body:
Who really benefits from the CIA chief’s Moscow trip?
Speculation abounds over the reason for CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent trip to Moscow. Which probably could have been an email. Or a social media post. Just like everything else this administration does.
Oooh, don’t tell me! He went to demand that Russian President Vladimir Putin not help Iran! Or he went to ask whether they’re still up for more speed dating to talk peace in Ukraine! Or maybe just to talk about swapping prisoners. Which happens fairly regularly. And doesn’t require a personal visit. Or maybe Ratcliffe just had a jonesing for that ice cream at the GUM mall in Red Square. Who really knows.
So I’d like to personally take the opportunity to add to the theories, which can only really be evaluated sometime down the road in hindsight.
The thing that strikes me the most about this trip is the sudden secrecy. Specifically from an administration with a penchant for blabbing about everything. If Trump wanted to tell Putin or Russian intelligence something, he’d do it himself on Truth Social Instead, he was uncharacteristically vague, calling the trip semi-routine. When is this guy tight-lipped about anything? It’s so far out of character for the American President that one is almost obligated to look for a motive for the secrecy.
So with that in mind, it seems reasonable to ask whether there is any financial or political constituency that stands to benefit from the message being sent by this unusually secretive trip.
Well, it turns out that it just happened to take place at the same time as the European Union was meeting to set its new 7-year budget, and Eastern European Baltic nations were making a massive push for cash from Brussels.
You know what they say: if you have a pet that starts in with some nasty habits, like chewing the furniture to get your attention, then you really have to nip that in the bud real quick. Otherwise, there’s a risk that, next thing you know, your other pets will learn from it and start gnawing on the couch or the table legs, too.
So here you have Europe, that’s been sitting there while Kiev says 'gimme money', and 'I deserve it because I’m defending all of Europe for you. Oh, and even better, actually, defending DEMOCRACY for you lazy bums'. And instead of whacking it on the nose and going, 'NO, BAD! Brussels just goes, 'Wanna treat?'
So now, what do you know, here comes Latvia, who’s been watching this whole charade, seeing that Ukraine goes from begging to getting tossed a bone every single time, and now they too are like, 'Woof, woof, I’m defending all of Europe for you. Where’s my money? 7 BILLION EUROS, specifically'.
And it’s not like Latvia is even bothering to come up with its own twist on Ukraine’s pitch. It’s not like they’re saying, 'Ukraine’s pitch to Brussels is, ‘Look, we’re being invaded. You’d better give us what we want because we’re the only thing standing between Putin showing up in Europe with a neck pillow for an Interrail tour of Europe.’ So we, Latvia, need to come up with something else. Especially since we aren’t actually being invaded – we just need some emotional-support money'.
No, instead, they’re just basically saying the exact same sort of thing minus the existential threat – that Latvia is the bouncer at the Baltic door keeping Putin on the other side of the velvet rope.
Surely it can’t possibly have anything to do with the fact that Latvia’s economy could use the kind of economic boost that can only come from having Brussels dump a ton of cash into its defense industry, right? Because everything’s going so well for Latvia economically, ever since this conflict in Ukraine went hot in 2022 and Riga cut itself off from Russian trade: from just over €2 billion a year back then, to just €193 million last year – an almost 90% reduction in the value of trade between the two countries, according to Latvia’s own foreign affairs ministry.
And now energy prices are going back up again, too – an 83% spike in gas prices since the beginning of this year in Latvia, and 24% over just the past month. An established trend since the EU cut everyone off from Russian fuel and now Trump’s cutting everyone off from fuel from the Middle East with his apparently endless 'mine’s bigger' standoff with Iran.
Oh look, here comes Lithuania now, too. What a surprise! Another guy watching from the cheap seats and going: 'Hang on. We’re also next to Russia. We have security problems, infrastructure costs, and defense bills. Where is OUR cash handout?'
Turns out that Lithuania has just gone directly to Brussels with the invoice, essentially saying: You keep telling us the eastern flank is crucial to European security. Wonderful. Please prove this commitment using the traditional European unit of measurement: euros.
When it comes to Eastern Europe, the EU’s seven-year budget plan is starting to look like a group dinner where everyone suddenly remembers that the guy at the end of the table has a corporate credit card.
But the real question is whose bills would Brussels ultimately be paying? Surely it’s just a mere coincidence that major beneficiaries of Latvian and Lithuanian defense spending include Trump’s America, as the largest supplier of major conventional arms to Latvia and Lithuania, according to the most recently available Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) arms transfer data.
All this comes after the western press reported that the CIA director flew to Moscow this week to tell Russia not to attack NATO countries. Which is actually great marketing for the cause of Eastern European countries shaking down Brussels and basically launching a grant program. They’re behaving now as though a potential future hypothetical Russian attack on NATO is serious enough to justify enormous new expenditures, but the benefit of Brussels’ largesse risks going to Washington as the top weapons supplier.
The trip is remarkably convenient for governments seeking to turn fears about Russia into a case for vastly increased European defense spending – and for the American defense industry that stands to benefit from a big chunk of that spending.
But hey, who really cares if everyone’s barking out for treats when you’re Brussels and all you ever need to do is reach into the pockets of the taxpayer. Even if you then run straight back to Uncle Sam with it and drop it in his lap.
