articles.title: Israel’s Shin Bet has held Russian-Israeli historian Artem Kirpichenok for more than a month without disclosing why. His family says the case may involve espionage.
articles.body:
Israel’s Shin Bet has held Russian-Israeli historian Artem Kirpichenok for more than a month without disclosing why. His family says the case may involve espionage.
Historian and writer Artem Kirpichenok flew to Tel Aviv on August 2 to attend an international conference, his support group said. Officers from Israel’s General Security Service (Shin Bet) detained him at the airport. Kirpichenok, a citizen of both Russia and Israel, has remained in custody ever since. Officials have not disclosed the reason for his detention.
Little is known about Artem Kirpichenok’s case. Israeli authorities may suspect him of espionage.
Family representatives told Meduza that, based on “unofficial information,” investigators suspect Kirpichenok of espionage and of contacting an agent of a foreign intelligence service.
But “there’s no Arab angle [to the case],” the source said. According to the source, the agent Kirpichenok allegedly contacted is not from Lebanon or Iran.
“Who could it be, then? If it’s Russia, the whole case is built on sand, as Israelis say. He’s a Russian citizen who has lived in Russia permanently since 2005. And Russia is hardly a stranger to Israel: the two countries conduct joint intelligence operations and share information despite friction over Iran and other issues,” the source told Meduza.
The alleged offenses are considered serious, according to the source, but even Kirpichenok’s lawyer does not know exactly what he is accused of. Israeli law has more than a dozen statutes that can apply in espionage cases, with penalties of up to life imprisonment.
“The fact that someone is held in a Shin Bet detention facility indicates that the person is suspected of crimes against state security,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family said.
A separate charge may stem from Kirpichenok’s 2018 trip to Iran, which he wrote about on social media at the time. Israel considers Iran an enemy state, and traveling there without special permission from the Israeli Interior Ministry carries a prison sentence of up to four years.
Nika Dubrovskaya, an artist and friend of Kirpichenok’s, told the outlet Bumaga that he visited Israel several times after his trip to Iran without running into problems at the border. Another friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza the account was accurate and said the historian had also visited Israel the previous winter, before his August trip.
He rented out his apartment in Ashkelon, which was one reason he returned to the country several times a year.
Kirpichenok’s research and columns
Kirpichenok, 51, holds a Doctor of Sciences degree and works as a journalist and researcher specializing in the Middle East and Central Asia. A family representative told Meduza that he is cautious — an “armchair scholar” who dislikes fieldwork.
A friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza that she met him in Israel in the mid-1990s, when she was living there and he was still studying at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She said that after he graduated, Kirpichenok could not find work in his field in Israel and was “very unhappy.”
Kirpichenok, a St. Petersburg native, returned to Russia in the 2000s and inherited an apartment there, she said. During those years, he worked as a tour guide, gave lectures, and wrote articles: “He worked with all kinds of publications and held, I’d say, Trotskyist views. Some minor grassroots activity: tours, and during COVID, he developed routes like ‘Sick Petersburg.’ A kind of intellectual precariat.”
Drawing on his dissertation about Hungarian nationalist movements at the turn of the 20th century, Kirpichenok wrote a book titled Vengriya-1956: drugoy vzglyad (“Hungary-1956: A Different View”). Kirpichenok criticized the 1956 Hungarian uprising, viewing it not as a progressive movement against the Soviet regime but as a far-right conservative revolt.
In recent years, Kirpichenok headed the Slavic studies department at the Center for Arab-Eurasian Studies, which was founded by Amr Abdel-Hamid, an Egyptian journalist, media manager, and former head of Al Jazeera’s Moscow bureau.
He also wrote about the Middle East for the Turkish broadcaster TRT and the Azerbaijani outlet Caliber, sharply criticizing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s actions in Gaza, and its policies toward Palestinians.
In his book Izrail’. Put’ k katastrofe (“Israel: The Road to Catastrophe”), Kirpichenok says Israel is not “the revived state of the Jewish people” but “the last bastion of Western colonialism.”
“Artem never wrote anything that went beyond what he read in the newspaper Haaretz and a couple dozen other sources, like B’Tselem,” his friend said. “I mean, some criticism of the existing regime. Geez, that exists in every country, and it’s a good thing — that’s what the intelligentsia is for.”
She was surprised by the possibility of espionage charges: “He doesn’t have any [classified] information. How would he have access to any?”
Kirpichenok flew to Israel for an academic conference — but officials in the city where it was supposed to take place had never heard of it
Kirpichenok is now being held in a Shin Bet pretrial detention facility in Petah Tikva.
He is alone in a cell where the lights stay on around the clock, with no outdoor exercise and no access to reading or writing materials. “All he can do in his cell is sit or lie down, sleep, or think,” a family representative said.
“Before October 7, 2023, only Arab Muslims were subjected to this kind of repression,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family told Meduza.
A support group of Kirpichenok’s friends believes the international conference may have been a trap set by security services to get the scholar into the country, according to the independent Russian outlet Doxa. Kirpichenok arrived in Israel on August 2 and had planned to leave six days later.
Representatives of Kirpichenok’s family contacted the municipality of the city where the conference was supposedly scheduled to take place, but officials there said no such event had been held. The family said Kirpichenok avoided answering questions about exactly who had invited him to Israel.
Israeli security officers pressured Kirpichenok, according to a family representative
The fourth court hearing in Kirpichenok’s case took place in Ashkelon on Thursday, August 27. The proceedings are closed to the public.
Kirpichenok was brought to court from the pretrial detention facility. Family representatives said he was held in a soundproof glass booth during the hearing. His lawyer, Inna Lebedinskaya-Katz, was unable to speak with her client during the proceedings, a Meduza source said. (Lebedinskaya-Katz declined to comment, citing a court order barring publication of details about Kirpichenok’s case.)
That day, the court extended the gag order on details of Kirpichenok’s case through August 31. A formal declaration of charges — roughly equivalent to an indictment in Russian legal procedure — was due to be filed on September 4. At that point, the defense would be able to access the investigation files, a family representative told Meduza. The family representative expects prosecutors to seek Kirpichenok’s continued detention through the end of the trial.
At the hearing, Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to exclude her client’s confession, arguing that Kirpichenok had been pressured into making it. Israel Shamir, a left-wing Israeli writer and columnist covering the case, said on Telegram that Lebedinskaya-Katz had filed the motion.
Kirpichenok had not been allowed to contact his lawyer, a family representative told Meduza. His only meeting with his defense attorney came on August 23, when he told Lebedinskaya-Katz that he had falsely incriminated himself “under pressure from investigators.”
During that meeting, Kirpichenok, in handcuffs, was held in a glass booth and spoke with his lawyer by phone. He feared the conversation might be monitored and worried that he would “be sent back down to the basement” where the interrogations took place, a family representative told Meduza.
Investigators allegedly threatened to confiscate his apartment in Israel and deport him to Ukraine. “He never supported the ‘special military operation’ that Russia launched, but because he holds left-wing views, he has spoken out against imperialism, including Russian imperialism,” a family representative told Meduza. There is no independent confirmation that investigators pressured Kirpichenok.
At the August 27 hearing, Kirpichenok “looked much worse” than he had when he met with his lawyer. According to Shamir, the defense attorney said: “His face seemed to sag, his eyes were dull, and he could barely smile.”
Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to move Kirpichenok from pretrial detention to house arrest because he has an apartment in Ashkelon, but the judge denied the request, citing the severity of the charges.
Kirpichenok also asked for an interpreter at future hearings — a request that surprised representatives of his family, since he had begun living in Israel as a teenager, served in the Israel Defense Forces, and later graduated from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The lawyer asked the court to allow a psychiatrist to see her client, citing his depressed state and post-traumatic stress disorder.
How Russia reacted to Kirpichenok’s detention
“The irony of Artem’s situation is that he holds two toxic passports. Neither country is particularly eager to stand up for him, you know?” the historian’s friend told Meduza.
Kirpichenok’s support group only recently contacted Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and Russian diplomats “have been emphatic in promising their support,” a family representative told Meduza. But because Kirpichenok also holds Israeli citizenship, Russian Embassy staff have not yet been allowed to see him.
Russia’s ambassador to Israel, Anatoly Viktorov, said the diplomatic mission “had sent a request to the appropriate Israeli authorities.”
Valery Fadeev, head of the Presidential Human Rights Council, sent a letter to Matthew Gillett, chair-rapporteur of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, on August 28. In the letter, Fadeev said: “In Israel, this kind of detention is usually linked to suspected crimes against state security.”
“This suggests that his detention was motivated by [Kirpichenok’s] political views,” the letter says. “Of particular concern is his health: he suffers from hypertension with a risk of retinal detachment, which requires constant medical monitoring.”
The Presidential Human Rights Council called on the United Nations to demand that Israeli authorities clarify the grounds for Kirpichenok’s detention and ensure that he has immediate access to a lawyer and qualified medical care.
Shin Bet had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment as of publication.

articles.title: Putin shows ‘saint-like patience’ – former US judge (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Putin shows ‘saint-like patience’ – former US judge (VIDEO)
Russia has the right to strike NATO plants making weapons for Ukraine, but President Vladimir Putin is showing great restraint to avoid a direct clash with the bloc, former American judge Andrew Napolitano has said.
Kiev has been launching hundreds of fixed-wing drones deep into Russian territory on a daily basis in recent months, many of which are manufactured in European countries. Earlier this year, the Defense Ministry in Moscow published a list of enterprises producing the UAVs, some of which are based in the UK, Germany, Italy, Czechia, and other NATO-member states. London and Paris are currently also discussing plans to make long-range SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine.
In an interview with RT on Friday, Napolitano, who hosts the popular ‘Judging Freedom’ interview channel on YouTube, said that “President Putin has demonstrated an almost saint-like capacity for patience and forbearance” by not ordering Russian forces to target those facilities.
“Under international law, he would have every right to strike at the munitions plants and the military, not the civilians… of the countries that are producing the weapons that are striking deep into Russia,” he said.
“I’m sure he understands that. My guess is that he’s considered it, but he’s been consistently patient. Sometimes even to the dismay of his strongest supporters,” the former New Jersey Superior Court judge added.
Putin is focused on the Ukraine conflict and “does not want a war against NATO,” he argued.
The Russian president previously labeled claims of Moscow having aggressive designs against the bloc as “nonsense,” saying that they are only made by Western politicians to distract the public from problems at home and justify growing military spending.
However, Moscow warned the UK in late August that its military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become legitimate targets for Russia if Kiev continues to use British-supplied weapons for strikes on Russian territory.
Russian officials also said that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly helped to facilitate Ukrainian drone attacks against northwestern Russia, Moscow could consider them complicit in those actions and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.
Napolitano said that the Ukraine conflict is “headed into an acceleration” and that he expects “a last-ditched effort by some of the NATO countries to try and prevent the inevitable, which is the achievement by the Russian military of its objectives.”
“The Ukrainians are aware that they’re on their last legs, so to speak, in the war. They know that their days are numbered,” he stressed.

articles.title: Zelenskyy accuses Russia of ‘demonstrative strikes’ on airports overnight ahead of US envoys’ Kyiv visit
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday accused Russia of carrying out “demonstrative strikes” on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of a planned visit to the Ukrainian capital by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy wrote on US social media company X.
He said Moscow deliberately targeted the airports “for the first time in a while.”
“Russian-Iranian ‘shaheds’ in response to American diplomacy,” he said. “We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.”
Zelenskyy said Kyiv would not allow threats to undermine diplomacy from its side, stressing that Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer.
“Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” he said.
Axios and Russian state news agency Tass reported, citing sources, that the two US envoys would visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.
Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner would visit Kyiv on Sunday after their trip to Moscow.
The two envoys have never visited Kyiv, while both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began.
Their latest visit was on Jan. 22, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.

articles.title: Senior US military staff subjected to polygraphs over Iran leaks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Senior US military staff subjected to polygraphs over Iran war leaks
The Trump administration has subjected around 50 military officers and civilian employees serving on the US Joint Staff to polygraph tests as part of an extraordinary effort to identify leaks to the press about the US-Israeli war on Iran, according to The New York Times.
Investigators questioned personnel in August over whether they had disclosed classified information to journalists, including information on dwindling US stocks of key munitions, the newspaper reported.
The Joint Staff — a Pentagon body of roughly 1,500 to 2,000 civilian and military personnel that supports the Joint Chiefs of Staff — is made up of senior officers who advise the president, defence secretary and National Security Council on military affairs.
The inquiry followed a succession of media reports warning that the months-long war has depleted US supplies of sophisticated weapons, including long-range missiles and Patriot air-defence interceptors used to counter Iranian ballistic-missile attacks.
Those reports have raised wider questions about Washington’s ability to sustain military operations in the Middle East while preserving its readiness for potential crises elsewhere. The conflict has also exposed the vulnerability of US troops, bases and allied infrastructure across the region to Iranian missile fire.
People familiar with the investigation told the NYT that the polygraph sweep appeared intended not only to identify officials who may have provided information to reporters, but also to deter other military personnel from speaking to the media.
The scale of the operation is highly unusual. Legal and military experts cited by US media said mass lie-detector testing has not previously been used so broadly, or at such senior levels, in the modern US military. CBS News reported that no one failed the questions specifically intended to establish whether they had leaked to journalists.
The investigation comes after US President Donald Trump intensified his attacks on reporting about weapons shortages and the conduct of the Iran war. Trump has branded media accounts of depleted US munitions supplies "treasonous" and said those responsible for leaks should be pursued.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the department does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters, but "takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly."

articles.title: Russia 'deliberately' targeted Kyiv, Boryspil airports ahead of US envoys' visit, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Russia 'deliberately' targeted Kyiv, Boryspil airports ahead of US envoys' visit, Zelensky says
Russia deliberately targeted airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of a planned visit by U.S. envoys seeking to advance peace talks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 5.
"Deliberately, for the first time in a long while," Zelensky said, describing the strikes as a response to discussions about the possibility of U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arriving in Ukraine by plane.
According to Zelensky, Kyiv International Airport and Boryspil International Airport were being discussed as possible arrival points in preparation for the U.S. envoys' visit.
Witkoff and Kushner are expected to visit Kyiv on Sept. 6 after traveling to Moscow as part of Washington's latest diplomatic push to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
"Russian-Iranian Shaheds in response to American diplomacy," Zelensky said, adding that Kyiv would adjust its operations regarding Russian airspace next week in response to the strikes.
Zelensky said Ukraine posed no threat to the U.S. delegation and remained interested in advancing peace efforts.
The strikes came as Ukraine proposed a temporary ceasefire to Russia ahead of the diplomatic visit.
Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov confirmed in comments to Suspilne on Sept. 5 that Kyiv had proposed a halt to both long-range strikes and hostilities along the front line.
Budanov said the proposal had been conveyed directly to Russian President Vladimir Putin, but Moscow had not responded.
The airport strikes were part of a broader Russian overnight attack. Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones against Ukraine, killing at least seven people and injuring at least 51 others.

articles.title: WATCH: CENTCOM strikes three Iranian oil tankers after IRGC attack on US ships
articles.body:
US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near Iran's key oil export hub.
The strikes were carried out after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships, CENTCOM said.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours," said Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US CENTCOM.
Tasnim, the semi-official Iranian news agency, reported earlier that four US missiles hit a tanker in the area of Kharg's anchorage. Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker's crew was being evacuated.
No American personnel were harmed, CENTCOM said.
There was no immediate official announcement by Iranian authorities.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth took to X to write, "If Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers. All they have to do is not shoot at [the] US Navy."
The exchange of attacks follows an escalation in the past week that threatens to deepen a conflict that has dragged on since the US launched strikes on Iran in February, disrupting global energy supplies and drawing opposition from a majority of Americans before congressional elections in November.
Trump threatens Kharg Island
US President Donald Trump said on August 31 in a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video that Kharg Island was being "blown to smithereens". Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90% of its crude via Kharg Island before the war, but flows have been disrupted since a US blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
Trump said on June 11 that he wanted to take over Kharg Island, but then said a threatened US military operation there was off the table for now, days before Tehran and Washington signed an interim agreement aimed at ending the war on June 17.
A US attack on Kharg would further pressure Iran's oil industry and its economy, which is already reeling from the US naval blockade.
The US imposed its blockade on Iranian ports after Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, an important waterway that carried one-fifth of the world's oil supply before the war.
Brent crude futures closed at their highest level since July 24 on Friday, at $96.28 a barrel, as tensions in the Middle East drive global supply concerns.

articles.title: Iranian leadership considers escalation as US officials fear military, cyberattacks - report
articles.body:
Iran may be considering a significant escalation in its war with the United States, having grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East, The New York Times reported on Friday, citing recent US intelligence reports.
Throughout the war, Iran gained a better understanding of its military strengths and confidence regarding its capabilities, leading to a reluctance among Iranian leaders to make any sort of agreement to fully end the war, according to the report.
In recent weeks, Iran has resumed strikes against US targets in the Middle East and the US has resumed strikes within Iran, but US officials fear that Iran may intensify their attacks both within the Middle East, targeting more ships in the Strait of Hormuz and US infrastructure in the region and within the cybersphere, mounting cyberattacks on essential US domestic systems, the NYT wrote.
Cyberattacks believed to have been perpetrated by Iran-linked hackers
According to the report, US officials believe Iran-linked hackers were behind cyberattacks on more than 100 water systems across the US in July.
While no systems were degraded to the point of making water unsafe to drink, the attacks caused disruptions that required manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories.
US oil and gas infrastructure may also be on the hackers' target list, current and former US officials told the NYT, although those systems are more protected.
It is unclear whether any energy systems have been breached, the NYT wrote.
In addition to any actual disruptions to US systems, former intelligence officials and security experts told the NYT that Iran may use the opportunity to increase the unpopularity of the war.
“Even if such attacks fail to meaningfully unsettle the American public, they can still play into a broader effort to exhaust domestic patience with this administration’s handling of the conflict,” Alex Orleans, a former US government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, told the NYT.
Iran has also gained a more precise understanding of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, and believes that US forces will not be able to sustain major new strikes due to dwindling munition stockpiles, according to the report.
Iran focuses on US elections
Additionally, knowing the war is unpopular, in part due to high gas prices, Iranian leaders may want to drag the war out until at least the midterms.
“The Iranians think they have maximum leverage,” the NYT cited Representative Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey, as saying. “So, from their perspective, why not keep sticking it to the president?”
Signs of Iran spreading propaganda against Trump have emerged, with Meta releasing a report highlighting a network of Facebook and Instagram accounts originating in Iran and focused on US politics, including "anti-Republican views."
Domestic media in Iran has also published more than 1,200 Persian-language articles within the past two weeks about Trump and the midterm elections, according to threat intelligence company Alethea.
While the Trump administration has focused on economic sanctions, one member of the Intelligence Committee told the NYT he expected Iran to endure the measures.
“Because the Iranian government does not care much about the suffering of its people, it has been able to withstand both punishing economic sanctions and military bombardments,” he was cited as saying.

articles.title: There are few signs that Iran is ready for a deal with the United States - NYT
articles.body:
There are few signs that Iran is ready for a deal with the United States - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
Iran may continue strikes in the Middle East for months. U.S. intelligence believes that sanctions could intensify the escalation.
Iran may be considering the possibility of escalating the conflict amid the resumption of mutual strikes with the United States in the Middle East. And little indicates that Tehran is ready to reach any deal with Washington. The New York Times writes, citing sources, UNN reports.
Details
"According to reports from U.S. intelligence agencies in recent weeks, Iran has become more confident in its ability to strike targets in the Middle East and, apparently, is determined to continue the conflict for several months in order to hurt the United States," the publication writes.
It is noted that, in many respects, these assessments reflect what is being observed on the ground, where hostilities have flared up again after a period of relative calm. Over the past week, Iran has attacked vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. forces in the region, while U.S. armed forces have carried out strikes on Iranian territory, resulting in the deaths of military personnel and civilians.
For now, the new clashes remain limited in scope. However, according to people who have reviewed the reports, they indicate that "Iran's hard-line government may be considering the possibility of a significant escalation of the conflict."
"Iran has emerged from a months-long war that started and stopped with a much better understanding of its military strengths and greater confidence in its capabilities," the publication adds.
Some current and former officials said the reports indicate that reaching any agreement on a complete end to the war will be difficult. According to some officials, "little indicates that Iran is ready to reach any deal with the United States, contenting itself with deepening President Trump's political problems ahead of the U.S. midterm elections."
At present, Trump is not seeking negotiations and has said that, in his view, he can apply economic pressure on Iran that will force Tehran to make concessions regarding control of the strait and, possibly, ultimately, its nuclear program. However, according to officials who have reviewed the intelligence reports, in the short term, U.S. economic sanctions are likely to continue provoking an escalation of the conflict.
"In the coming weeks, Iran may take actions similar to those it took in July. At that time, Iran attacked U.S. military bases in the Middle East, killing three Americans in Jordan; struck shipping in the Strait of Hormuz; and also attacked infrastructure in Kuwait and elsewhere," the publication's sources said.
We remind you
White House chief Donald Trump said that the renewed U.S. campaign against Iran would not last "too long".

articles.title: Russia Strikes Ukrainian Airports, Infrastructure Ahead of U.S. Envoys' Visit
articles.body:
Russia hit Ukraine's airports in the capital Kyiv and the nearby town of Boryspil ahead of visits to Moscow and Kyiv by U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. But Zelensky said that officials had discussed the possibility of Witkoff and Kushner using a plane for their expected visit to Kyiv on Sunday.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelensky said on Telegram. “Russian-Iranian Shaheds (drones) in response to American diplomacy.”
Elsewhere, a Russian ballistic missile strike on a Ukrainian steel plant in the eastern Dnipro region killed five people, damaged production facilities and infrastructure, forcing a halt to all operations, steel producer Metinvest said on Saturday.
“This is yet another attack on a civilian Metinvest steelmaking asset and further evidence of Russia’s systematic strikes against Ukraine’s industrial base,” the company said in a statement. It said the Kamet Steel plant produced pig iron and steel exclusively for civilian purposes.

articles.title: Air Defense Forces down 128 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air Defense Forces down 128 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Friday, September 4, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh regions, as well as 167 Shahed combat drones (about half of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the directions of Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, drone-system units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:30 on Saturday, September 5, Air Defense Forces had shot down or suppressed 128 drones.
Hits by missiles and attack drones were recorded at 23 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at one location.
In addition, some of the weapons failed to reach their targets; information about them is still being clarified.
The attack is ongoing, with enemy drones still present in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, four people were killed and five others injured in a Russian attack on Kamianske in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

articles.title: The US called on Ukraine and russia to suspend strikes during Witkoff’s and Kushner’s visits to moscow and Kyiv — media reports
articles.body:
The US called on Ukraine and russia to suspend strikes during Witkoff’s and Kushner’s visits to moscow and Kyiv — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
Witkoff and Kushner will visit moscow and Kyiv to resume peace talks. The US called on the parties to temporarily halt strikes.
The United States is insisting that the Ukrainians temporarily halt their drone attacks on moscow and the country's energy facilities, and that the Russians halt their missile attacks on Kyiv during the visit of U.S. President's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to the capitals of the russian federation and Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the NYT.
Details
Two of U.S. President Donald Trump's top emissaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are heading to moscow and Kyiv this weekend to resume negotiations on a peace deal that would end the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine, officials familiar with the diplomatic efforts said.
Witkoff, the American leader's special envoy, and Kushner, his son-in-law and frequent key negotiator, are expected to meet with Russian President vladimir putin on Saturday. They will then travel to Kyiv for the first time to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
According to officials, talks over the trip have been underway for weeks, with the United States insisting that the Ukrainians temporarily halt their drone attacks on moscow and the country's energy facilities while the two men are in russia, and that the Russians similarly halt their missile attacks on Kyiv. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a trip that has not been officially announced.
The publication notes that it is unclear whether the Americans are offering both presidents new proposals or pushing them to narrow the gap on the remaining issues, including who will ultimately control the Donbas, Ukrainian territory partially occupied by russia.
Although Witkoff and Kushner have traveled to moscow several times, they have not been to Kyiv, despite numerous official invitations. Two weeks ago, CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited moscow, where he stayed for only a few hours to meet with his Russian counterpart. Witkoff has seen putin more than half a dozen times.
The meeting is taking place at a dangerous moment in the conflict. For much of the year, Ukraine's attacks on oil refineries and other energy targets have had a devastating impact, forcing Russians to stand in line for hours to get gasoline, if they can find it at all. But the Ukrainians have run out of interceptor missiles to stop Russian missiles raining down on Ukraine, leaving Kyiv and some other cities almost defenseless.
President Trump has sought to bring russia back into the fold: he and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent invited russia to take part in the Group of 20 finance ministers' meeting last week in North Carolina, despite objections from European allies. russia has been excluded from many diplomatic meetings since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
To remind
Zelenskyy stated that U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would visit moscow on Saturday and that Ukraine guarantees the "normal functioning of Russian airspace," while they are expected in Kyiv on Sunday.
Context
Back in July, it was reported that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner agreed to visit Kyiv for the first time as part of peace efforts to end the war.
At the end of August, it was reported that Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Ukraine, amid intensified russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv, had been postponed but not canceled.
On September 3, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that a visit by U.S. President's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv could take place in the coming days, but that they would first visit moscow.
On September 3, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced "new momentum" in peace efforts to end russia's war against Ukraine, with the return of an active political and diplomatic phase, but noted that achieving this without the participation of the American side was unrealistic.
On September 4, a source in the Russian media reported that American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would visit Russia and Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, September 5 and 6.

articles.title: Scott Bessent met with Russia’s finance minister. Then he said Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites were helping fuel a global ‘energy shock.’
articles.body:
Scott Bessent met with Russia’s finance minister. Then he said Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites were helping fuel a global ‘energy shock.’
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure one of the causes of the global energy crisis. He spoke after a meeting of G20 finance ministers in North Carolina, to which Anton Siluanov, Russia’s finance minister, was invited for the first time since the start of the war.
“Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products,” Bessent said on Fox News, adding that the attacks were contributing to an energy shock and putting upward pressure on prices globally. He also cited the U.S. war with Iran, but stressed that the conflict would come to an end.
Siluanov’s presence at the summit — and his bilateral talks with Bessent — drew criticism from Ukraine’s allies. Anton Gerashchenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, pushed back on Bessent’s remarks, arguing that his framing transforms Ukraine “from a victim of Russian aggression into a cause of a global problem” and “reverses cause and effect.” The energy crisis, he said, is driven primarily by wars, and the U.S.–Iran conflict has had a far greater impact on global markets.
Gerashchenko stressed that the United States wants to cut Russia’s energy revenues without reducing Russian energy supplies to global markets, and that rising gas prices ahead of November’s midterm elections have forced the Trump administration to find a “convenient explanation.”
Those elections and fears of another spike in fuel prices have already slowed passage of a new sanctions bill targeting Russia in the House of Representatives, Bloomberg reported.
The bill was drafted by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. It would allow the United States to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas — chiefly China, India, and Turkey. The Senate passed it by an overwhelming majority in August, but the House has been less receptive, with lawmakers concerned that removing Russian oil from the global market could push gas prices even higher amid the war with Iran.
Ukraine is trying to persuade Congress not to delay the sanctions. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s commissioner for sanctions policy, traveled to Washington this week to meet with members of Congress and said Ukraine was “quite optimistic” about the level of support for the bill. “Everyone agreed that it was necessary to increase pressure on Russia,” Vlasiuk said. “No one said that he definitely would not support this bill.”
The European Union, meanwhile, is weighing new restrictions on Russia. After Germany blamed Moscow for a failed drone attack at Leipzig Airport, European diplomats plan to discuss curbing tourist visas for Russians, restricting Russian diplomats’ travel within the EU, and sanctioning additional vessels in Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Bloomberg reported.
The war in photos: Brovary, Kyiv region
Industrial sites in the Brovary district of the Kyiv region have been burning for a second straight day after Russian strikes. A drone hit a Coca-Cola plant on September 3, and warehouses caught fire after another strike on the morning of September 4.

articles.title: Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workers
articles.body:
On the evening of 1 April 2024, a team of aid workers from World Central Kitchen (WCK) stood on Gaza’s Mediterranean shore overseeing the unloading of a barge full of desperately needed food on a makeshift jetty made of sand and rubble.
The Gaza war had been raging for six months and Israel’s closure of land crossings had left the whole territory facing the threat of famine. WCK and local Palestinian contractors had constructed the jetty out of everything they could lay their hands on, including debris from the bombed house of one of the contractors, so that the pallets of humanitarian assistance could be delivered by boat from Cyprus.
A consignment of 200 tonnes of rice, flour and other proteins had arrived two weeks earlier, the first sea shipment to dock in Gaza since 2007. This was the second shipment and it was even bigger, with enough food to prepare more than 1m meals, as well as a Ramadan gift of dates from the United Arab Emirates.
The choreography of the delivery had been coordinated over several days with the Israeli army, and an officer was on the jetty to observe the proceedings. In the midst of a devastating bombing campaign after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023, this humanitarian effort was supposed to be carried out under internationally agreed military protection.
The shipment had been unloaded by 8.30pm but despite the lengthy planning, there was a delay in receiving final Israeli security clearance for the eight hired trucks and two WCK escort vehicles to leave the jetty. By the time the green light came from local Israeli commanders and the convoy began to move south, night had fallen.
There was no initial overhead surveillance but two drones joined somewhere along the route to the first stop, a WCK welcome centre 6 miles to the south. Those drones were assigned to the Israel Defense Forces’ (IDF) Nahal brigade, which had not been fully briefed on the aid convoy’s itinerary.
A special adviser assigned by the Australian government to assess the case (in the interests of justice for the Australian victim Lalzawmi Frankcom), found that “specific details about the pre-coordinated WCK aid mission had not been passed down from higher levels of Southern Command to the brigade and UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operator”.
Local guards
At the WCK welcome centre, a few local men hired as guards were waiting, at least one of them armed. At a time of widespread hunger, many food convoys had been mobbed by desperate crowds as well as organised gangs, some of whom may have had been linked to Hamas, though Hamas never had the grip on food deliveries alleged by the Israeli authorities.
Using local security for aid deliveries was not unknown in Gaza, but it was directly against WCK policy to use armed escorts. The WCK says it is unclear why the local team on that night agreed to accept armed guards. The official Israeli version of events suggests it was “due to the convoy’s delayed departure, during night-time hours,” and noted it “was not coordinated with IDF authorities”.
The official Israeli version does not say how many armed men were waiting for the convoy (unofficial versions vary between two and four), but drone footage reportedly showed one of them climb on top of the cabin of one of the trucks and fire a shot in the air shortly afterwards, for reasons that remain unknown.
The Nahal brigade officers and the drone operators assigned to them concluded it was a Hamas hijack, based in part on the false assumption that such hijackings were commonplace.
“The troops also identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organisation had taken control of the convoy,” the official account says.
The Israeli military prosecutor’s version of events, published last month to justify his decision not to pursue criminal proceedings, does not mention the breakdown in communication between the army’s coordination and liaison administration, which handles humanitarian needs in the territory, and the Nahal brigade controlling that sector of the Gaza Strip.
Furthermore, the prosecutor’s version says efforts by IDF personnel to contact WCK were unsuccessful. But according to WCK sources and the Australian report on events, contact was established that night with WCK headquarters in the US, which in turn got in touch with an employee in Gaza.
According to the Australian report, the WCK worker on the ground told headquarters staff the guards only had “fake guns”. It remains unclear what the basis for that claim was, but the WCK assured the IDF that it had not lost contact with the convoy and it had not been hijacked.
Arrival at destination
It is unclear whether this exchange with WCK was relayed to the Nahal brigade before the strikes. But even if it was not, the fact that the convoy of eight food trucks continued on its journey and arrived at its intended destination, the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, should have been ample proof that the aid had not been seized by Hamas.
The military prosecutor’s summary acknowledges that the “convoy arrived at the designated warehouse and unloaded the aid” but does not address the seemingly straightforward conclusion that it had therefore not been diverted. The IDF has yet to release audio recordings of military communications that night.
After the trucks entered the warehouse, the WCK workers and the local guards stayed outside by their own vehicles for about 10 minutes. That short period, observed by operators of Israeli drones, appears to have helped seal the aid workers’ fate. As far as the Nahal brigade’s chief of staff, reserve Col Nochi Mendel, was concerned, they were “mingling” with Hamas.
Under the very loose procedures of “incrimination” that delegate much to the discretion of field commanders like Mendel, the WCK workers became unwitting targets as they celebrated the completion of a successful delivery of aid, because they were in the proximity to armed men.
“There was incrimination. The incrimination was according to the rules,” Mendel said. “There were armed men there with certainty. With certainty, they [the aid workers] had mingled with armed Hamas men.”
Other IDF officers have confirmed to the Guardian that such a process of guilt by association is used widely to determine targets, though different field commanders use different standards in making decisions. The Israel military prosecutor, in making his assessment on criminal responsibility, did not address the practice of incrimination in targeting.
Parting of ways
After the brief pause outside the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, the guards and the WCK workers went in separate directions. “The WCK vehicles departed together west towards the coast. Concurrently, the vehicle containing the locally contracted security personnel, including the previously identified gunmen, drove north,” the Australian report says. It also makes clear that the IDF was aware of this parting of the two groups.
“One UAV tracked the locally contracted security vehicle heading north for approximately three minutes until it arrived at another warehouse where up to four gunmen were identified exiting the vehicle and entering the building,” the report says. “A decision was made to discontinue targeting them due to the time available before they entered the northern warehouse.”
The military prosecutor’s version makes no mention of this drone or the fact that the suspected gunmen were seen driving off in a different direction and entering a separate building. It claims instead that “several individuals mistakenly … identified as armed persons” were observed getting into WCK vehicles.
That is at odds with the Australian report and the accounts of Israeli officers familiar with the investigation. They said a bag was spotted by a drone operator being put in a WCK car, and that the operator mistook it for a gun, though sources briefed on the drone video said that later analysis showed no sign of a suspicious bag.
Whether or not it was a gun was irrelevant as far as Mendel was concerned. He saw his task as carrying out the government policy of crushing Hamas governance in Gaza, which included stopping its seizure of aid deliveries.
“If a Hamas operative takes over a truck and after that he sells it and that’s how he recruits more people, then what does it matter if he’s armed or not?” Mendel said.
In its economical, dry prose, the Australian report describes what happened next as the WCK workers left the warehouse at about 11pm. “The WCK vehicles proceeded west to the coast. Due to the time delays encountered, rather than return to the WCK welcome centre as planned, a decision was made to return directly to the accommodation in Rafah,” the report says.
“After turning south on to the coast road, the three WCK vehicles were struck in relatively quick succession, each strike being approximately two minutes apart. There were two survivors from the strike on the first (up-armoured) vehicle who quickly moved to the second vehicle, then two survivors from the second (up-armoured) vehicle who moved to the third vehicle. There were no survivors from the third (soft-skinned) vehicle. Over the four-minute period 23:09 – 23:13, the seven WCK workers were killed – likely one in the first vehicle, two in the second and four in the last.”
The seven victims of the IDF drone strikes were from the UK, Australia, Poland, Palestine and the US. The Britons John Chapman, James Kirby and James Henderson were working as security consultants. Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, a Palestinian driver and translator, was the youngest killed, at 25. Frankcom, Damian Soból, a Pole, and Jacob Flickinger, a US-Canadian dual citizen, were humanitarian workers for WCK.
The military prosecutor claimed that in turning south towards Rafah, the WCK workers were “deviating from the route that the organisation had coordinated in advance with the IDF”, giving weight to the Nahal brigade’s mistaken impression that “Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy”.
Mendel also mentioned this “deviation” as a mitigating factor. However, the Australian report found that the fact that the WCK workers had changed their route only became known after they were killed, and “as such it did not play a factor” in the decision to open fire.
The official Israeli version of events says Mendel and his brigade fire support commander ignored an order on the night of the airstrike from a superior officer to cease any attacks on humanitarian convoys, but Mendel has said the order is a fabrication.
“It never happened, never existed,” Mendel said. “No operational directive reached the brigade to cease the strikes … We checked it a thousand times.”
In explaining his own decision-making, Mendel stressed he was carrying out Israeli government policy by stopping Hamas taking control of food deliveries. He had been lauded by his superiors for ordering strikes on several earlier alleged Hamas attempts to hijack aid. In his mind, the events on the night of 1 April 2024 fitted the same pattern.
“I didn’t plan to kill the aid workers,” Mendel said, but added: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”
Justifying this conclusion, he said: “They were mixed together with Hamas operatives …near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on.”
In a written statement, WCK said: “It is extraordinary to learn now that some in the IDF considered our humanitarian work to be enemy activity based on the flimsiest evidence, or no evidence at all.
“This undefined, unjustified and unlawful view is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. The IDF’s shifting excuses and explanations for these unlawful airstrikes are precisely why we continue to demand an independent investigation with the full release of the IDF’s evidence.”

articles.title: Budanov: Ukrainian ceasefire proposal conveyed to Russian leadership, no response received
articles.body:
Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov reported that Ukraine sent a ceasefire proposal to the Russian side, which was conveyed to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, but no reaction followed from Russia.
In a comment to Suspilne, he emphasized that the proposal pertained not only to strikes on Ukraine, but also to combat operations on the front lines.
"Drones are flying – you saw everything," Budanov noted.
He also confirmed that the visit of U.S. President's special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Ukraine will take place on September 6, speculating that Russians might refrain from attacking Kyiv due to this. Budanov also stated that Witkoff and Kushner would arrive in the RF "in just a few hours."
As reported, Witkoff and Kushner plan to visit Kyiv on Sunday, September 6, following another trip to Moscow. Trump stated that Kushner and Witkoff are bringing a peace proposal with them. At the same time, according to diplomatic sources, prospects for reaching agreements on ending Russia's war against Ukraine during Trump's envoys' visit to Moscow are viewed extremely pessimistically in Russia, as Russian leadership is ready to end the war only on Russian terms.
Earlier, media and bloggers, citing sources in the security sector, reported that Ukrainian units allegedly received instructions to observe a regime of silence from September 5 to September 8 on land, in the air, and at sea. Interfax-Ukraine had no official confirmation regarding the receipt of such an order by the Defense Forces. Following continued shelling from Russia on September 5, the Armed Forces of Ukraine issued a statement declaring that they continue to perform designated tasks for Ukraine's defense according to plan, and a unilateral ceasefire is impossible due to the risk to the life and health of military personnel.

articles.title: Iran accuses US of missile strike on tanker near Kharg Island
articles.body:
Iran accused the United States of striking an Iranian tanker near the country's main oil export hub of Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf on Saturday, raising fresh concerns about an escalation in the conflict between Tehran and Washington.
The semi-official Tasnim news agency, citing a correspondent near Kharg, reported that the tanker was hit by four U.S. missiles near the island's anchorage, about 6 miles (10 kilometers) from the coast. The crew was being evacuated and there were no reported casualties, Tasnim said.
Other Iranian media outlets also reported explosions near Kharg Island, but details about the incident remained unclear. The semi-official Fars news agency said explosions were heard in the area but that there was no visible smoke and the source of the blasts was unknown.
State-affiliated Nournews reported unconfirmed information from local sources that an Iranian tanker had been hit by a U.S. missile near Kharg. The Asr Iran news site said the tanker had been struck by four projectiles and was being unloaded.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the reports. Iranian authorities had not issued a formal statement, while U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Kharg Island is Iran's main crude oil export terminal and a strategically important part of the country's energy infrastructure. Before the war, Iran shipped about 90% of its crude exports through the island, according to Iranian reports. Those shipments have been heavily disrupted since the United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian oil exports in mid-April.
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened action against Kharg Island. On Aug. 31, he posted a one-line message on social media accompanied by an AI-generated video saying the island was being "blown to smithereens."
Trump had also said June 11 that he wanted to take control of Kharg Island, although he later said a planned U.S. military operation there was off the table for the time being. The comments came shortly before Tehran and Washington signed an interim agreement on June 17 aimed at ending the war.
Any confirmed U.S. strike on Kharg would place additional pressure on Iran's already strained oil industry and economy. Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and relies heavily on oil revenue.
The confrontation has also disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global energy route that carried about one-fifth of the world's oil supply before the war. Iran effectively closed the waterway, prompting the United States to impose its blockade on Iranian ports.
A confirmed attack on Kharg could also increase the risk of further Iranian retaliation against U.S. forces and American allies across the Middle East.
The reported tanker strike came as violence continued elsewhere in the Middle East.
In Yemen, Iranian-backed Houthi rebels accused government forces of killing at least three people in airstrikes in the western and southwestern parts of the country.
The attacks Friday occurred in Hodeida and Taiz provinces as Yemen's military said it carried out more than 15 airstrikes against Houthi positions along front lines in the two provinces.
Houthi authorities in Hodeida said a father and daughter were killed when their home in the southern Jarahi district was struck. In Taiz, a shelling attack killed a man and wounded another, according to the Houthi-run al-Masirah satellite news channel.
The violence comes as fighting between the Houthis and government forces has intensified along Yemen's western coast near a strategically important supply route.
In southern Lebanon, the Health Ministry said Israeli strikes killed three people and wounded nearly two dozen others in southern Lebanon and the eastern Bekaa Valley.
The Israeli military said it carried out strikes against Hezbollah positions late Friday after the Iran-backed group launched a drone toward Israeli forces in southern Lebanon. The drone was intercepted and no Israeli soldiers were injured, the military said.
Lebanon and Israel signed a U.S.-mediated framework agreement in June under which Israeli forces would withdraw from areas they occupy in southern Lebanon in return for the disarmament of Hezbollah. But implementation has made little progress.
The latest Israel-Hezbollah conflict began after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in the days following the launch of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran on Feb. 28. Israel subsequently invaded Lebanon and has maintained control over a large area of the country's south.
Hezbollah has strongly opposed direct talks between Lebanon and Israel.
The situation remained fluid Saturday, with reports of fighting and military activity continuing across several parts of the region.

articles.title: France Warns of Consequences for Leipzig Airport Attack
articles.body:
French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot stated that European nations will respond with consequences to hybrid attacks following the explosive drone strike on Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport.
In a statement published by the French Embassy in the US, Barrot outlined three principles regarding the current security situation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He asserted that Russia remains the sole aggressor since the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine and emphasized that European countries have not initiated actions against Moscow.
Addressing the Leipzig incident, Barrot characterized the deployment of an explosive-laden drone against infrastructure as a severe escalation.
He stated that the EU and NATO will respond when the integrity of their infrastructure, electoral systems, or democratic foundations is compromised.
Barrot also drew a distinction between the Russian government and its populace. He noted that Russian citizens are experiencing domestic rationing, economic constraints, and casualty rates of approximately 35,000 soldiers per month as a direct result of the Kremlin’s policies.
Rising sabotage incidents across Germany
The French minister’s remarks follow a confidential assessment by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), which recorded 165 suspected sabotage cases and 747 suspicious drone flights nationwide during the first eight months of 2026.
The BKA report, compiled through the GAZ-Hybrid threat response center, detailed 24 formal espionage investigations and 112 espionage-related crimes, including the unauthorized surveillance of military facilities and defense equipment.
Analysis: Pro-Russia AfD Eyes First German State Government as Support Surges
While the BKA did not collectively attribute all 165 incidents to Moscow, German authorities have previously accused Russia of directing the failed August drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Recent domestic security investigations also include early September attacks on electrical substations in Brandenburg and North Rhine-Westphalia, where unidentified perpetrators used launched projectiles to cause high-voltage short circuits.
Additionally, authorities reported an August incident in Lower Saxony where suspects assaulted a security guard who was investigating drone activity over a natural gas processing facility.
Earlier in July, police in Bavaria arrested a Moldovan national suspected of operating a drone over the defense manufacturer KNDS on behalf of Russian state agencies.

articles.title: Zelenskyy after speaking with Trump envoys: Ukraine prepared to halt strikes on cities involved in talks
articles.body:
Zelenskyy after speaking with Trump envoys: Ukraine prepared to halt strikes on cities involved in talks
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated, following a conversation with US President Donald Trump's special envoys, that Kyiv is willing to halt airstrikes on the cities involved in the peace process.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media
Quote: "I have just spoken with the US President's envoys. They have already begun working with the Russian side today.
From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process. From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."
Details: Zelenskyy announced that a plan has been approved for diplomatic meetings with the US delegation on Sunday 6 September.
Quote: "We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation."
Background:
- Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ukrainian authorities had sought to establish a temporary ceasefire along the line of contact ahead of the visit by Trump's special envoys. Ukraine's defence forces were ordered to observe a ceasefire from 00:00 on 5 September until 23:59 on 8 September. Russian forces thwarted this plan.
- Ukraine's General Staff later said that fighting is continuing along the line of contact because the Russians have not stopped their attacks on Ukraine.
- Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office, later confirmed that the ceasefire proposal had been conveyed to Putin, who had not responded.
- On the afternoon of 5 September, the Kremlin announced that Vladimir Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting from midnight.
- The US president's special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Moscow on Saturday. The US negotiators are expected to arrive in Kyiv on Sunday.
