articles.title: Europe stockpiled Leopard 1s for a war that never came. Ukraine is rebuilding them for this one.
articles.body:
- Ukraine is getting 170 Leopard 1A5 tanks from a European consortium
- Most fight as tanks, but some are becoming air defense vehicles—built in Rome, paid for with frozen Russian money
- A second program swaps in an unmanned Belgian turret and drops the crew to three
- Europe's warehouses hold enough spare hulls to feed both
Ukraine has lost a quarter of its German-designed Leopard 1A5 tanks. But it could get many more of the nimble, 40-ton tanks. And some could have brand-new turrets that make them lighter, faster, farther-shooting, and more survivable.
The hulls are 1980s West German. The refurbishment is done in Germany, the air defense turrets are built in Rome, the tank turrets are designed in Belgium, and one of the two programs is paid for out of frozen Russian assets. Ukraine's newest armored vehicles are being assembled from the leftovers of a war Europe spent forty years preparing for and never fought.
In 2023, a German-Danish-Dutch consortium pledged 170 Leopard 1A5s to Ukraine. The 1980s-vintage tanks have come from German, Danish, and Belgian surplus stocks.
Refurbished in Germany by tank-maker Rheinmetall and fitted with add-on anti-drone armor in Ukraine, the first 135 or so Leopard 1A5s now equip at least five units: the 44th Mechanized Brigade, 5th Heavy Mechanized Brigade, the 425th Assault Regiment, the 142nd Mechanized Brigade, and the 13th National Guard Brigade.
Losses have been heavy. The Russians have struck no fewer than 37 of the four-person tanks, destroying at least 30 of them. The 44th Mechanized Brigade, which is fighting a defensive action south of the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, has been hit the hardest. The brigade has written off around half of its original allotment of 31 or so Leopard 1A5s.
Another 35 Leopard 1A5s from the 2023 pledge should eventually reach Ukrainian units, potentially making good those losses.
But Kyiv is diverting some of those initial 170 Leopard 1A5s to a pair of conversion programs that are reinforcing Ukraine's air defense while also re-equipping the ground forces with a new generation of tank.
The first conversion program, overseen by Rheinmetall, plucks the old turrets with their 105-millimeter cannons off some Leopard 1A5s and drops in a new turret with a faster-firing 35-millimeter anti-aircraft gun. Effectively a next-generation Gepard, the resulting Skyranger 35 is a mobile, armored drone-killer that can post up between Russian drone launch sites and Ukrainian cities in order to down incoming Geran drones before they can strike.
Its revolver cannon fires 1,000 rounds a minute out to 4 km, using airburst ammunition that scatters tungsten pellets in the path of an incoming drone. An unnamed EU country is paying for the systems out of proceeds from frozen Russian assets, and Rheinmetall builds them at its subsidiary in Rome. Germany's own army has ordered 19 and is discussing hundreds more; Ukraine's arrived first.
The first imagery of a Skyranger 35 in Ukrainian service circulated online this week, with the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment.
Old tank, new turret
The second conversion program won't produce combat-ready vehicles for another year or so. This program will swap out the turrets on 31 Leopard 1A5s. The new turret, produced by John Cockerill Defense in Belgium, is unmanned: the commander and gunner move down into the hull alongside the driver, and an autoloader replaces the human loader. That drops the crew from four to three and takes everyone out of the part of the tank most likely to be hit.
The new turret is welded from ballistic aluminum instead of steel, shaving three tons off the tank's 40 and freeing weight for reactive armor, anti-drone netting, or electronic warfare kit.
As a bonus, the 105-millimeter gun in the multi-million-dollar Cockerill 3105 turret also elevates far higher than the gun in the existing turret—42 degrees, against roughly 20 on the original. That confers greater range when a tank functions as artillery, firing its cannon at targets over the horizon: Cockerill says no other Western main battle tank can shoot indirectly the way this one does, and Ukrainian trials reached 10 km from a covered position.
Kyiv has ordered 30 of the turrets and holds one more it bought for testing last year. Some time in 2027, that is a battalion of new medium tanks: a cutting-edge turret on a chassis built when Leonid Brezhnev was alive.
To provide hulls for the 31 Cockerill-converted Leopard 1A5s while also sustaining the Skyranger 35 program, Ukraine must make a choice. Combined, the two programs need potentially 50 or more tank chassis, but just 35 Leopard 1A5s from the initial 170-tank pledge are still in the queue for delivery to Ukraine.
Russia took the cages off its newest tanks. The new Arena-M shield bought them a few minutes.
Ukraine's ground forces are already short on tanks; taking Leopard 1A5s from the five brigades and regiments that operate the type could deprive those units of desperately needed firepower. Fortunately for Ukraine, there are still hundreds of old Leopard 1A5s in warehouses in Europe and farther abroad—and Rheinmetall is pulling the Skyranger hulls from storage rather than from Ukraine's active fleet.
Trending Now
French historian Stevius made a count and concluded "the stocks in Europe are far from exhausted." As recently as 2022, German firm Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft held 99 Leopard 1A5s. Rheinmetall held 88 of the tanks in 2022 and, in 2023, bought 50 more from OIP Land Systems in Belgium. That's 237 tanks: 67 more than the Europeans pledged to the Ukrainians in 2023.
Some of those 67 excess Leopard 1A5 hulls are unusable owing to rust and other wear and tear. Even so, there should be enough Leopard 1A5s left in Europe to feed the Skyranger and Cockerill conversion efforts. And once those run out, there are still some ex-Italian and ex-Greek Leopard 1A5s that Ukraine could acquire.
And if it can secure the financing, Ukraine could convert those additional tanks—or even some of its existing ones—into faster, farther-firing Leopard 1A5s with Cockerill C3105 turrets. Cockerill has already proposed doing the whole active fleet, around 100 tanks.

articles.title: Putin announced battlefield encirclements that the evidence doesn’t show, but Russia’s real offensive is accelerating elsewhere
articles.body:
Putin announced battlefield encirclements that the evidence doesn’t show, but Russia’s real offensive is accelerating elsewhere
At a late-night press conference in Bishkek on September 1, Vladimir Putin said what he believed was happening on the battlefield. Once again, his account clashed with the Russian military’s documented gains. Putin is evidently aware that even troops at the front do not accept his reports, so he cited sources in the General Staff and “other agencies.” He said the picture, as it “appears” to him, is “fairly objective.” He immediately said that Ukrainian units had been encircled in two places in the Kharkiv region and that Sviatohirsk, near Sloviansk, had been captured. The claims surprised even the people behind Telegram channels close to the Russian military command, who likely work at the headquarters of the units responsible for the sectors Putin mentioned. Yet, strange as it may seem, Putin’s optimism about these operations is not detached from reality: Russia’s offensive accelerated in late summer and again pushed Ukrainian defenses into crisis along several important axes in early fall.
The Kharkiv region
- Putin said several thousand Ukrainian troops were encircled near Vovchansk and pinned against the border. Russian forces have indeed broken through from two directions southeast of the city, which Russia captured by mid-2026 after two years of heavy fighting. One group advanced from Vovchansk in the north and approached the large settlement of Bilyi Kolodiaz; another is advancing toward it from the Russian border to the east.
- Russia’s Defense Ministry said a month ago that Bilyi Kolodiaz had also been captured. Since then, however, published videos filmed by Russian units have shown strikes on Ukrainian positions inside the settlement. The nearest Russian positions are in tree lines several kilometers to the north.
- Published videos indicate that the force advancing from the east has not moved past Kupyne, 25 kilometers (16 miles) from Bilyi Kolodiaz.
- To be fair, the most recent videos from the area date to mid-August, and the situation may well have changed considerably in the weeks since. Still, it would be unusual for such changes to leave no visual trace at all — the Russian push toward Bilyi Kolodiaz in early August and the Ukrainian counterattacks that followed were both well documented.
- In any case, Russia does not have enough troops in this sector to encircle a 25-by-25-kilometer (16-by-16-mile) area. No encirclement of that size has been completed since May 2022, despite many attempts by both sides.
- An encirclement of Ukrainian units near Pisky-Radkivske, south of Kupiansk, seems even less likely. The Ukrainian army has maintained a large bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Oskil River for four years, centered on Borova, north of Pisky-Radkivske. Ukrainian forces also have numerous crossings over the shallow Krasnooskilske Reservoir. From the bridgehead, they periodically attack near the junction of the Kharkiv and Luhansk regions, trying to keep a small part of the Luhansk region under Ukrainian control so Russia cannot capture the entire region. Overall, this stretch of the front remains a “backwater.” Most troops in the area are fighting either near Kupiansk to the north or near Lyman to the south.
- Russian forces have made gains around Kupiansk and inside the city in recent months, retaking territory Russia lost during Ukraine’s counteroffensive last winter. They have also seized large areas on the eastern bank of the Oskil between Borova and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi. But Putin said last fall that Russia already fully controlled Kupiansk, so this time he did not mention these actual gains. Nor did he mention a new Ukrainian attempt to pressure the northwestern flank of the Russian force advancing on Kupiansk near Dvorichna and Zapadne.
Lyman and Sviatohirsk
- Putin said Russian forces had captured Sviatohirsk, a city on the northern bank of the Siverskyi Donets River, 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Sloviansk. But no Russian positions have been documented in the immediate vicinity of Sviatohirsk in recent months. Moreover, Ukrainian forces have rolled back Russian incursions into the nearby villages of Yarova and Pryshyb, on a small Russian bridgehead on the river’s southern bank.
- Ukrainian forces are also trying to push Russian troops farther from Lyman, a city Russian forces tried and failed to storm in early summer.
- Overall, Ukrainian forces have managed to halt the Russian advance toward Sloviansk on the river’s northern bank, but not on its southern bank.
Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Dobropillia
- After capturing most of Kostiantynivka — where scattered groups of Ukrainian troops still remain — Russian forces found themselves in early August in a situation they had hoped to avoid. Despite their success in the center of the front, which stretches more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the Siverskyi Donets River to Pokrovsk, they could not advance directly on the Kramatorsk–Sloviansk urban area. Attacks on the flanks — the Pokrovsk–Dobropillia, Dobropillia–Druzhkivka, and Lyman–Sviatohirsk sectors — were stalling, and a direct push toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from Kostiantynivka or Chasiv Yar was difficult without support from the flanks.
- In recent weeks, Russia’s offensive on the western flank, from Dobropillia to Druzhkivka, has intensified sharply.
- Russian forces captured settlements south of Dobropillia and then reached Annivka on the city’s eastern outskirts. Exactly a year after a failed attempt to break through to the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road, Russian troops struck again at the same point, this time with far larger forces and more extensive preparation. They captured Kucheriv Yar — which Russian forces had also occupied in August–September 2025 — and Rubizhne. Farther east, Russian forces also pushed toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road, reaching the area around Novoandriivka.
- Russian forces continue to advance toward Druzhkivka along the Kazennyi Torets River. They have crossed the river and taken up positions in Raiske, 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the city. Along the entire stretch from Dobropillia to the northwestern approaches to Druzhkivka, Ukrainian defenses are in a full-blown crisis requiring urgent measures — such as redeploying major reserves, as Ukraine did in the same area a year ago.
- The situation is also deteriorating southeast of Druzhkivka, where Russian troops are advancing rapidly — by the standards of this war — from the direction of Chasiv Yar. They have already reached Izhivka on the approaches to Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka.
- Farther north, on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets, Russian forces have reached the outskirts of Mykolaivka, which shields Sloviansk.
- The two sides’ starting positions for the battle over the Kramatorsk–Sloviansk urban area will depend on how Ukrainian commanders respond to these advances from several directions. A delayed or inadequate response could mean the battle begins as early as winter. Kyiv has created new command structures but has not yet transferred additional troops, which could be freed up only by weakening other sectors of the front. Ukrainian forces in the northern Donetsk region are clearly feeling the absence of an army corps — an air assault formation. The formation was sent southwest in the spring to the junction of the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk regions to stop the Russian advance deeper into the Zaporizhzhia region, particularly toward Orikhiv.
Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka
- In August, Ukrainian forces made another attempt to advance near the junction of the three regions. They broke through near the Donetsk–Zaporizhzhia road and advanced 10–12 kilometers (6–7 miles) to the Mokri Yaly River. The breakthrough point seemed well chosen: it was right at the junction of the Russian “Vostok” and “Tsentr” groups, bringing Ukrainian troops onto the western flank of the “Tsentr” group’s 90th Tank Division, whose positions faced north.
- Russian commanders, however, quickly brought in forces from the 90th Tank Division and the neighboring 41st Combined Arms Army to repel the Ukrainian attack from the west. In mid-August, both sides published videos showing their flags raised in about 10 villages. Ukrainian forces did so first, followed by units of the “Tsentr” and “Vostok” groups. The situation has remained unclear since then, but the lack of new information suggests that the Ukrainian advance was stopped, perhaps only temporarily, and that Ukrainian forces lost some of the territory they had previously retaken.
- Ukrainian forces also failed to achieve the offensive’s primary goal. Strikes on the northern flank of the “Vostok” group, which began in the spring, were meant to halt its advance eastward toward Orikhiv, in the central Zaporizhzhia region. The advance was only slowed, and it has now resumed with renewed force.
- Russian forces have reached the Orikhiv–Novomykolaivka road in several places. It is one of the main supply routes for the Orikhiv garrison. Russian troops have often failed to hold positions along the road or in nearby villages, however: Ukrainian forces continue to hold positions behind and on the flanks of the advancing Russian troops and are even counterattacking.
- The clash between small groups of assault troops on the steppe has already had dire consequences for Orikhiv itself. The “Dnipro” group’s 42nd Motorized Rifle Division had failed for two years to break through the Novodanylivka–Mala Tokmachka line south and southeast of Orikhiv; it did so in just two weeks. Russian forces have captured all of Novodanylivka, and assault troops from the 42nd Division have also established positions on the southern outskirts of Orikhiv.
- For the first time in a long while, Russian assault troops have also reached the center of Mala Tokmachka, a large village familiar from its frequent appearances in reports by pro-war commentators. Russian troops have cut the road from the village to Orikhiv. It remains unclear whether the 118th Mechanized Brigade, which had held Mala Tokmachka since early 2024, managed to retain positions even on the village’s outskirts. With Russian forces in their rear and the road to Orikhiv cut, doing so will be extremely difficult.
How territorial control has changed
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Zelensky Approves Response Plans After Russian Strikes: ‘We Will Choose the Right Time’
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday that he had approved proposals from Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) and the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) to respond to Russia’s continuing strikes on Ukrainian cities, warning that Kyiv would choose its own time to retaliate.
“I approved the proposals from the Security Service of Ukraine and the Armed Forces of Ukraine for responses to the strikes the Russians are carrying out against our cities,” Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 4.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Our warriors will find a way to respond to Russia for all of this, and we will choose the right time to respond,” he added.
Zelensky cited Russian strikes throughout the day on Kyiv and the Kyiv region, as well as Kharkiv, Sumy, Kherson, Odesa and cities in the Dnipro and Donetsk regions.
He said 12 people had been injured in Kyiv at the time the address was recorded. The toll later rose to 15, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
One of Friday’s most significant attacks targeted the headquarters of the SBU in central Kyiv.
A Russian drone struck the office of Oleksandr Poklad, the acting head of the SBU, in a building on Volodymyrska Street opposite St. Sophia Cathedral. Poklad was not in the office at the time.
Zelensky earlier said the drone had been aimed directly at Poklad’s office and instructed the security chief to prepare an “appropriate, tangible response” to the attack, adding that Ukraine’s military would support it.
Russian Attack Sets Nine-Story Residential Building Ablaze in Boryspil
Russia launched a Kh-31P missile and 121 drones against Ukraine from the evening of Sept. 3 into Sept. 4. Ukraine’s Air Force said 103 drones were shot down or suppressed, while strikes were recorded at 15 locations.
The promise of retaliation came as Kyiv prepares for another round of US-led diplomacy aimed at ending Russia’s war.
Zelensky said US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Moscow before visiting Kyiv on Sunday.
Ukraine will refrain from air strikes affecting Russian airspace while the US negotiators are in Russia to ensure their safe arrival, Zelensky said, while demanding Moscow reciprocate during the diplomatic mission.
“There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same,” Zelensky said.
He said Kyiv wants the talks with the US delegation to be “as constructive and substantive as possible” and would assess both the proposals brought by Witkoff and Kushner and Moscow’s response to them.
“We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill three: ministry
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Five killed in Israeli attacks across southern, eastern Lebanon
Israeli strikes in southern and eastern Lebanon late on Friday killed at least five people and injured 24, the Lebanese health ministry said.
The ministry said in a statement that strikes hit five locations in the southern Tyre and Nabatieh regions and the Bekaa region in the east.
It updated an earlier toll given by Lebanese official media which had reported two of the deaths in the south.
The strikes came despite a truce between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah group.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported the strike hit near the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, which the Israeli army said it had captured, though Hezbollah did not confirm losing it.
Two young men were targeted while riding a motorcycle in the city of Nabatieh, NNA said, adding that rescuers transported their bodies to a local hospital.
Israel announced on Thursday it had taken control of the ridge. Defence Minister Israel Katz said the military would work to "prevent the enemy from re-establishing itself in the area".
Israel stepped up strikes in the Nabatieh region on Friday and also targeted the village of Rmadiyeh in the Tyre area, located more than 10 kilometres from the Israeli border.
The ministry said the third person was killed and 15 others hurt there, including two children, three women and six rescuers.
A rescue service source earlier told AFP that the strike in the village, which is sheltering people displaced from other southern areas, had hit a house.
Israel and Hezbollah have been trading fire since March when the group dragged Lebanon into the wider Middle East war by attacking Israel in support of Iran.
Israel responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
The conflict has calmed since a US-Iran memorandum of understanding and a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon was agreed in June, but Beirut still reports Israeli strikes.
Imran Riza, the UN humanitarian coordinator for Lebanon, said on X on Friday that families returning to Nabatieh following the truce "face widespread destruction, lack of basic services, ongoing insecurity and uncertainty".

articles.title: U.S. forces destroy three Iranian oil tankers
articles.body:
- CENTCOM disabled or destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on September 5 after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships, which evaded the attacks unharmed.
- The strikes follow a pattern since February's Operation Epic Fury, including a fragile June ceasefire and a July strike on more than 80 Iranian targets.
U.S. Central Command forces struck and disabled three Iranian oil tankers on September 5, hours after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships patrolling the region, according to a CENTCOM statement.
Both American vessels, an aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, evaded the Iranian missiles, and no U.S. personnel were harmed, CENTCOM said. The command did not name the two ships involved.
In response, American forces permanently disabled two Iranian crude oil carriers, the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and completely destroyed a third, the unladen M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM said forces struck the Kylo in multiple critical locations after its crew was ordered to abandon ship, rendering the vessel inoperable.
CENTCOM described the three tankers as part of what it called a multibillion-dollar shadow fleet that generates revenue for the IRGC and its regional proxy groups, adding that Iran had no way to defend the ships once they were targeted.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
The strikes are the latest exchange in a conflict between the United States and Iran that began February 28, when the U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury. American forces have since enforced a naval blockade meant to cut off Iran’s oil exports, repeatedly disabling tankers that attempted to defy it. In May, an F/A-18 launched from the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) disabled the tanker M/T Hasna’s rudder with cannon fire near an Iranian port, and jets from the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) later disabled two more unladen tankers, the M/T Sea Star III and M/T Sevda, attempting the same route.
A ceasefire took hold by early June, though CENTCOM described it as fragile at the time and publicly disputed Iranian claims that its forces had fired on U.S. Navy ships in the Gulf of Oman, saying doing so would have violated the truce. The uneasy calm broke down further in July, when Iran struck three commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, prompting CENTCOM to hit more than 80 targets across southern Iran overnight, including air defense systems, command-and-control networks, coastal radar sites and more than 60 IRGC small boats.

articles.title: Ukraine Defence Contact Group to meet next week, says Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukraine Defence Contact Group to meet next week, says Kyiv
Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara and his German counterpart Boris Pistorius have held a phone call, during which they discussed preparations for a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format) to be held next week.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Khmara briefed Pistorius on Russia's ever-intensifying air terror, emphasising that the key threats are jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles.
Khmara said Ukraine is developing its own defence plan and taking asymmetric action that is yielding results. Meanwhile, strengthening protection against Russian strikes as quickly as possible remains a priority.
The two sides discussed funding for defence needs. Ukraine's Defence Ministry is conducting an audit of resources and human capital within Ukraine's defence forces. However, financial support from Kyiv's partners remains critically important to Ukraine's resilience.
The ministers also focused on preparations for the Ramstein-format meeting next week and discussed closer cooperation between the Ukrainian and German defence industries.
Khmara thanked Germany for its significant support and leadership in working with other partners of Ukraine.
Background:
- The last meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group was held on 18 June at NATO Headquarters in Brussels and was co-chaired by the United Kingdom and Germany.
- Following the meeting, Pistorius announced that Ukraine would receive a three-digit number of air-to-air missiles from German stocks. He also said the two nations would jointly produce ground robotic systems.
- On the same day, Ukraine and Germany signed a defence agreement concerning the joint development of an air defence system capable of intercepting ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Chants, applause, and hundreds of supporters: A report from the Moscow courthouse where children’s hospice founder Lida Moniava faced a charge of spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military
articles.body:
Chants, applause, and hundreds of supporters: A report from the Moscow courthouse where children’s hospice founder Lida Moniava faced a charge of spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military
On the evening of September 3, Simonovsky Court placed Lida Moniava, founder of Dom s Mayakom (“Lighthouse Charity Foundation”), under a set of restrictions in a criminal case accusing her of spreading “fake” information about the Russian military. Moniava is one of the leading figures in contemporary Russian philanthropy: she founded the Dom s Mayakom charity and its hospices for children with severe and incurable illnesses. Dozens of people came to Simonovsky Court in Moscow to support her. The news outlet Bereg recounts what happened — and shows how Moniava’s supporters celebrated her release. Meduza is translating the report in full.
A hearing on pretrial restrictions for Lida Moniava, founder of the Lighthouse Charity Foundation, is scheduled for 5 p.m. on September 3. A full hour before the hearing, Muscovites who have come to support Moniava are already gathering outside the Simonovsky Court building.
Police searched Moniava’s home early on the morning of August 2 as part of a criminal case over spreading “fake” information about the Russian military, then arrested her. The case stems from a post Moniava published on her Telegram channel to mark the first anniversary of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “For a year now, my country has been sending missiles, tanks, and soldiers into Ukraine. For a year now, innocent people have been dying because of it,” she wrote.
A short young woman named Nadezhda stands in the parking lot reserved for official vehicles directly in front of the courthouse. She is visibly nervous. She introduces herself as Moniava’s goddaughter.
“I’m waiting for justice. If someone like Lida is sent to prison, something truly terrible will happen to the world,” Nadezhda says.
A mixed crowd gradually gathers by the parking lot: young people who might be described as part of the alternative scene, middle-aged people, and elderly members of the support group. Some call themselves Moniava’s friends and acquaintances; others, like red-haired Makar, dressed all in black, learned about her from recent news coverage.
“When I read about Lida, I realized she’s just an incredibly good person — kind, with the noblest intentions,” Makar tells the independent Russian outlet Bereg. “Of course, it’s a real shame things turned out this way.”
Makar says he is trying not to get his hopes up that the charges against Moniava will be dropped or that she will be released from custody, “so I don’t end up disappointed.”
Mikhail, an acquaintance of Moniava’s, is also there to support her. He speaks about her much as dozens of others have in Facebook posts supporting her over the past day.
“I admire what she does, what she stands for, and the fact that she’s open about it. That’s genuinely brave,” Mikhail says. “You can do charity work and still be a conformist because you think charity makes up for everything. But Lida did good work without becoming a conformist just to keep doing it.”
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moniava stayed in the country and continued helping children with incurable illnesses. She also set up a fund to help refugees from Ukraine and Nagorno-Karabakh, as well as residents of the Kursk region’s border areas affected by the Ukrainian military’s incursion in August 2024.
While helping people affected by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Moniava also wrote antiwar posts on Facebook. In February 2026, Russian authorities fined her 45,000 rubles for “discrediting” the Russian military over those posts. She wrote about children killed in a Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih and the deaths of the Martynenko family — a father, a mother, and their 11-year-old son — in a strike on Sumy.
After the February hearing at which a judge imposed the fine, Moniava thanked her followers for their support and said in a post that she had “received a lot of advice to leave Russia”:
When Center E is banging on your apartment door, it’s scary, of course. But look at this photo — Anya and I are having such a great time on our shift [at the hospice]. She’s a girl who spent 19 years behind the walls of a residential institution. If I leave, children in palliative care will spend more time in residential institutions and intensive care units. I doubt I could live happily in some other country knowing that. So emigration isn’t in the plans.
In the same post, Moniava added: “I also can’t stay silent as if there’s no war. Trying to live honestly comes first for me.”
Natalya, who came to Simonovsky Court, does not know Moniava personally but has long followed her work. “I’m just in shock over what’s happening,” she says. “It’s probably to be expected, but it’s still very hard for me to accept. I’m an outsider looking on, and I simply respect her work, so I came here to support her. Lida is a wonderful person who helps others live and survive. That’s very important in our world. In turbulent times, we need to support each other somehow and do something.”
Others who came to support the Dom s Mayakom founder included Nobel laureate Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta; Nyuta Federmesser, founder of the Vera Fund, which helps people with incurable illnesses; actress Tatyana Drubich, co-chair of the same fund; and Daniil Maksimov, a Vera Fund employee and founder of an inclusive magazine about sex for people with disabilities.
Maksimov, a blogger, writes on social media about living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and the problems wheelchair users face. Several people in motorized wheelchairs gathered outside Simonovsky Court on the day of Moniava’s hearing.
The Lighthouse Charity Foundation needs support. In recent days, it has lost many donations and some of its donors. You can donate from Russia in rubles on the foundation’s website.
Shortly before 5 p.m., a prison transport van parked outside the courthouse pulls away. By now, around 200 people have gathered. Someone in the crowd says, “This one’s probably leaving now, and the next one will have Lida in it.” When another prison van drives onto the court grounds soon afterward, people start chanting, “Lida! Lida!”
The van’s barred windows make it impossible to see who is inside. The van pulls into the garage.
People line up to enter the courthouse, and the line moves very slowly. One woman in a blue jacket stands out among the crowd, holding a copy of Viktor Vilisov’s book Nas Vsekh Toshnit (We’re All Sick to Our Stomachs) with a bright orange cover. Off to one side stands Yekaterina Duntsova, head of the Rassvet (“Dawn”) party; somewhere in the same crowd are Tatyana and Valery Yashin, the parents of convicted politician Ilya Yashin, who was sent to Germany in a prisoner exchange.
“So many people showed up. This is a really high-profile case,” someone in the crowd says.
“Yeah, this isn’t Remeslo.”
Forty minutes later, the line still has not cleared. Two young men carrying tripods come out of the courthouse toward the line. Someone in the crowd asks hopefully:
“So, any news?”
“No, nothing at all.”
It is a little after 5 p.m. when Nyuta Federmesser, who had entered the courthouse near the front of the line, comes back outside. “Lida hasn’t arrived yet,” she says. “We came down because it’s impossible to breathe in there. There’s no point in standing here anymore because they’ll start kicking everyone out soon. The court closes at 6 p.m.”
Some of those who came are in no hurry to leave, even though it is very stuffy inside. Dmitry Muratov takes a spot right by the courtroom entrance. One woman who came to support Moniava offers people postcards to write warm messages on, which will later be delivered to Moniava. A police officer comes upstairs and asks everyone to leave the building: the court has closed for the day.
Everyone heads down to the courtyard, which is packed with people. In the middle, a group shares a pie. Police soon drive everyone out of the courtyard as well, and the gates close. Now everyone waits for Moniava by the fence.
Traffic police officers watch the crowd from cars with their emergency lights on. One of them approaches the crowd. What he says is familiar from rallies and pickets:
“Citizens, do not obstruct the passage of other citizens!”
“We’ve heard that one before,” a woman over 60 says. “I’m so sick of you!”
Word eventually spreads that Moniava has been brought to the courthouse after all and that the hearing has begun. The press is not allowed to attend.
“I know Lida personally,” says Fatima, who came to Simonovsky Court to support her. “Lida is a wonderful person. She’s done a lot in our country to help children with severe and incurable illnesses, and she built a palliative care system. Of course, it’s pretty horrifying that she’s inside the Simonovsky Court building at all.”
Neither Fatima nor Mikhail, who respects Moniava for refusing to conform, expects “anything good” to come of the judge’s decision.
Half an hour later, the crowd starts to stir. The courthouse doors open, and two security officers appear in the doorway. Several people start chanting “Lida!” but she is nowhere in sight. A few men come out, followed by a woman. “The workday is over,” someone in the crowd says.
As they wait, someone starts singing, but the words are impossible to make out.
Finally, Moniava’s defense attorney, Mikhail Biryukov, says from inside the courtroom that the court is releasing Moniava from custody and placing her under a “ban on certain activities.” While the investigation continues, she is barred from going outside between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., communicating with witnesses, or using the internet.
Sometime between 8 and 9 p.m., Moniava and Biryukov emerge from the courthouse. The people waiting behind the fence chant Moniava’s name and applaud. Once outside the gates, she tells the crowd: “I thought I was going to get 10 years in prison. Some kind of miracle.”
She says investigators spent “many hours” trying to persuade her to admit guilt: “For some reason, it’s very important that the defendant say they feel guilty. I don’t feel guilty. I want the war to end as soon as possible.”
“Is there anything you want to do right now?” journalists ask Moniava.
“See my friends,” she says with a smile.

articles.title: Finland Holds Largest Civil Defense Drill Since WWII
articles.body:
Finland has staged Europe’s biggest civil defense exercise since World War II, putting thousands of people through crisis scenarios amid growing concern over a Russian military threat and suspected sabotage across Europe.
More than 2,000 people, including volunteers, students and military conscripts, took part in the two-day Shelter 2026 exercise, held earlier this week in the central Finnish city of Kuopio.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The drill centered on Luola, a vast underground sports complex built into rock that was converted into a civil defense shelter.
Participants rehearsed how authorities would respond if cyberattacks knocked out electricity and water supplies, alongside a scenario involving possible missile strikes from Russia.
The exercise also tested coordination between authorities, businesses, schools, volunteer groups and local residents during a major emergency.
Finland, which shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia, joined NATO in 2023 following the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, ending decades of military non-alignment.
Russia threat looms large
The drill comes amid heightened concern across Europe over Russian military activity, cyberattacks and suspected sabotage.
Last month, a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft was suspected of entering Finnish airspace over the Gulf of Finland for around three minutes, penetrating roughly 8.7 kilometers into the Nordic country’s territory.
France Warns of Consequences for Leipzig Airport Attack
Finland summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which came less than three months after another suspected violation involving a Russian military aircraft.
The airspace violations come against a backdrop of growing concern over suspected Russian hybrid operations elsewhere in Europe.
Germany this week accused Moscow of orchestrating an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August, where an explosives-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. Russia denied responsibility.
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said this week that a fire at a factory supplying drone components to Ukraine was an act of sabotage, although Polish authorities have not publicly identified who was behind it.
Long history with Russia
For Finland, concern over its much larger eastern neighbor is deeply rooted in history.
The Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939, starting the Winter War. Despite being heavily outnumbered, Finnish forces resisted for 105 days before a peace treaty ended the fighting in March 1940.
Finland retained its independence but was forced to cede 11% of its territory to the Soviet Union. More than 25,000 Finns were killed and around 44,000 wounded.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on Ukrainian airport shelling: Russian-Iranian Shaheds are answer to American diplomacy
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized the Ukrainian side's interest in ending the war while commenting on overnight shelling by Russian occupiers, but stressed the necessity of holding the enemy accountable.
"Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer. Russia will answer for what it is doing. Thank you to everyone who helps our state and Ukrainians," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Saturday.
He also reported that overnight the enemy delivered demonstrative and targeted strikes on Ukrainian airports in Kyiv and Boryspil.
"Obviously, such Russian strikes on airports are a reaction to the discussion and preparation of the possibility for the American side to use a plane to arrive in Ukraine and land at 'Kyiv' airport or 'Boryspil' airport. Russian-Iranian 'Shaheds' in response to American diplomacy," the president said.
He promised to take this into account when planning strikes against the Russian Federation. "We recorded this Russian step, and next week we will accordingly adjust our operation regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous due to the presence of drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, on our side there are no threats to diplomacy and there will be none," Zelenskyy added.
As reported, representatives of US President Donald Trump, Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner, plan to visit Kyiv on Sunday, September 6, following another trip to Moscow. "Today it has already been clearly determined that American representatives will be in Ukraine and in Russia in the coming days. Details are available from the team of the President of America. We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and will visit Kyiv on Sunday," Zelenskyy reported on Friday.
Trump stated that Kushner and Witkoff are bringing with them a proposal regarding the termination of the war. At the same time, according to diplomatic sources, in the Russian Federation the prospects for reaching agreements to end the war of the Russian Federation against Ukraine during the visit of Trump's special envoys to Moscow are assessed as extremely pessimistic, as the Russian leadership is ready to end the war only on Russian terms.

articles.title: Ukraine ready to halt strikes on cities involved in US-mediated peace talks: Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that his country is ready to halt strikes on cities involved in US-mediated efforts to negotiate a settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy said he spoke with US envoys who traveled to Moscow for talks earlier in the day and that they had already begun their work in Russia.
“From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process.
“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,” Zelenskyy added.
The Ukrainian president’s statement came after the Kremlin said Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered a three-day halt to strikes on Kyiv beginning at midnight local time (2100GMT).
Earlier Saturday, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow for talks aimed at finding a settlement to the more than four-year conflict.
The US envoys are expected to visit the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Sunday for the first time following their Moscow trip.
Trump said Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would travel to Moscow not with new ideas, but with a proposal aimed at ending the war.
“They’re bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” Trump said, referring to the two negotiators.

articles.title: Fresh Yemen clashes kill more than 60
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Fresh Yemen clashes kill more than 60
Fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the country's Houthi rebels killed more than 60 people on Saturday, including civilians, medical and military sources told AFP.
The renewed clashes in Yemen's southwest over control of a gateway to the Red Sea came after Friday saw some of the deadliest fighting in years, following the collapse in July of a 2022 ceasefire.
According to three Yemeni military sources, 26 government troops were killed during several hours of fighting in the country's southwest, while medical and military sources from the Iran-backed Houthis said 31 rebel fighters were killed.
One medical source in the government-held city of Taiz said a missile strike also killed six civilians travelling by bus and wounded seven others.
A government official blamed the strike on the bus, travelling between Taiz and the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government in Aden, on the Houthis.
In Taiz, a military officer said the "coming hours will be decisive" after the Houthis seized positions near the city a day earlier.
The officer added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden in response to the Houthi offensive, which aims to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab strait.
On Friday, the fighting killed 129 people, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
With Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships, the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint has gained importance as a transit route for oil from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude.
A military official told AFP on Saturday that three airstrikes by Saudi Arabia, a key backer of the government in Aden, had targeted positions recently captured by the Houthis in Taiz.
In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and Yemen's government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to the capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks.
The fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and government troops supported by US ally Saudi Arabia signals the emergence of a new front in the wider Middle East war, which broke out in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
The Houthis have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have begun targeting its ships and territory.

articles.title: Trump says U.S. may strike Iranian nuclear site soon, calls conflict "small potatoes"
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military may soon strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain -- a fortified site near Iran's Natanz enrichment facility -- while trying to downplay the conflict with Iran as "small potatoes."
"We may hit Pickaxe very soon," Trump told reporters at the White House, referring to the underground facility where Washington says Iran has moved some of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Meanwhile, Trump tried to downplay the conflict with Iran, arguing that it was not a war. "It's a military conflict, but it's very intermittent," Trump said, though he has repeatedly described the conflict as a "war" while avoiding the term at times.
"I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," Trump claimed.
"I would say that it's intermittent. You know, we do intermittent strikes," Trump said. "There's a lot of truth that we're not fighting right now. There's no fighting."
U.S. forces targeted nearly 60 Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz this week, including air defense sites, radar systems, mine-laying capabilities and communications facilities, CNN reported.
On Tuesday night, a U.S. strike hit a wedding party in Sirik County in Hormozgan province, killing at least five people and injuring over 60 others, Iranian state media reported.
Trump on Wednesday threatened to launch more strikes on Iran "anytime we want."
The United States and Israel launched massive military attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, marking the start of a conflict that has killed thousands of people. ■

articles.title: US reportedly put 50 military and civilian officers on lie detectors over Iran war leaks
articles.body:
US investigators in August administered polygraph tests to 50 military officers and civilian officials following leaks concerning depleted American munitions stocks amid US war on Iran, according to multiple US media reports.
The probe targeted personnel with the Joint Staff, a group of senior military leaders advising the president, focusing on leaks regarding shortages of long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors due to the war with Iran, The New York Times reported.
A CBS News report revealed that the FBI was not involved in conducting the tests, as the military utilised its internal investigators.
Not all senior leaders were tested, with the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine being excluded from the sweep.
US President Donald Trump is said to be furious about the unauthorised disclosures.
Those subjected to polygraphs were questioned on whether they leaked information to journalists regarding critical ammunition shortages amid tensions between the US and Iran.
No officials failed the polygraph questions designed to determine if they leaked information to the media, according to CBS News.
Pentagon refuses to speak on probe
Investigators were also concerned about whether a government official was potentially operating as a foreign spy because access to the specific munitions data was highly restricted, it said.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the agency "does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters" but takes classified leaks "extremely seriously and investigates accordingly."
Trump denied the reported strategic shortages, insisting the military possesses "massive amounts" of weaponry.
Trump labelled the disclosures as "treasonous statements" and "fake news," warning that those responsible would be "hunted down" and face severe prison sentences.
The polygraph sweep followed separate unauthorised disclosures, including a leaked portion of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book.
The document showed six four-star leaders formally expressing dissent about extending the war against Iran, warning it is "unsustainable" and erodes global readiness.
Parnell condemned the leak as a "crime" and "a betrayal of the force" and said much of the reporting was inaccurate.

articles.title: Putin pauses strikes on Kiev
articles.body:
Putin pauses strikes on Kiev
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered a three-day hiatus in strikes on Kiev ahead of talks with senior US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who arrived in Moscow earlier on Saturday.
The negotiations are expected to focus on resolving the Ukraine conflict. Witkoff and Kushner are slated to visit Kiev after their meetings in Moscow, which include talks with Putin.
Speaking on Saturday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that “Russian president [and] commander-in-chief Putin has ordered [the armed forces] not to conduct strikes on Kiev for three days starting from midnight today.” He added that the decision was intended to allow Witkoff and Kushner to hold negotiations with Ukrainian officials in the country’s capital.
Several Ukrainian media outlets carried reports earlier in the day, saying that Kiev’s forces had been instructed to hold their fire starting from Saturday midnight until Tuesday.
Ukrainian broadcaster Suspilne subsequently quoted Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff Kirill Budanov as saying that Ukraine had sent a truce proposal to Russia calling for the temporary cessation of hostilities along the front line, as well as all air strikes. However, Moscow did not respond, according to Budanov.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump said that Witkoff and Kushner were “bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” without elaborating on the specifics.
Since the start of Trump’s second term in office in early 2025, the two negotiators have repeatedly visited Moscow as part of the US president’s efforts to mediate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine.
However, despite a glimmer of hope following last year’s meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska, the diplomatic back-and-forth has since stalled as neither Russia nor Ukraine will compromise on key issues.
Still, speaking on Thursday, the Russian president praised Kushner’s and Witkoff’s work, saying that the US negotiators are “always welcome guests here, and we work with them with pleasure.”

articles.title: In Germany, production of thousands of long-range drones for Ukraine has begun—one of them can strike at a distance of 1,500 km
articles.body:
In Germany, production of thousands of long-range drones for Ukraine has begun—one of them can strike at a distance of 1,500 km
Kyiv • UNN
Auterion Airlogix will produce 5,000 drones for Ukraine by 2027. Anubis has a range of up to 1,500 km and a 40–50 kg warhead.
The American-German-Ukrainian company Auterion Airlogix has launched serial production of 5,000 Anubis and Seth-X drones for the Defense Forces of Ukraine. This was reported by Defense Express, according to UNN.
Details
Production was launched at a plant near Munich. The contract is worth approximately €300 million, with funding provided by the German government. The order is planned to be completed by mid-2027.
Under the joint project, Auterion is responsible for the software, while the Ukrainian company Airlogix is responsible for the hardware of the drones.
What is known about Anubis and Seth-X
Anubis belongs to the class of long-range strike drones. According to Defense Express, it has a range of up to 1,500 km and a warhead weighing 40–50 kg. The company also emphasizes that the drones are adapted to operate in conditions of intensive use of electronic warfare systems.
Less is known about the Seth-X. It is designed to engage personnel, lightly armored vehicles and logistics vehicles at medium range.
Both models have already been documented in use by Ukrainian military personnel. Anubis has appeared in official materials from the Unmanned Systems Forces, as well as in photos from the Russian side.
In the future, the company plans to open another plant in eastern Germany. According to Defense Express, the project will provide Ukraine with an additional production line for strike drones, while giving Germany the opportunity to strengthen its own defense-industrial potential at the same time.

articles.title: Aeon discloses new specs for its Zeus tactical missile
articles.body:
- Aeon disclosed new details about its Zeus tactical missile, including a stated speed exceeding Mach 0.65 and a 6-pound warhead payload, in a LinkedIn post.
- The company has said Zeus costs roughly $50,000 per unit and holds eight-figure contracts with the Department of War, though new specifications remain unverified.
Aeon, a Texas-based defense manufacturer, disclosed new technical details about its Zeus tactical missile system in a public post from Chief Growth Officer Wes Shover, including a stated speed of more than Mach 0.65 and a 6-pound (2.7-kilogram) warhead payload.
The Defence Blog first reported on Zeus in April, when Aeon founder and CEO Naweed Tahmas gave an exclusive look at the system, describing it as a software-defined, modular guided weapon priced at roughly $50,000 per unit, with a target production rate exceeding 10,000 units a year. Zeus sits in the same rough weight class as an unguided AT4 rocket but is designed to deliver precision guidance closer to a Javelin-class system, at a fraction of the cost of legacy anti-armor missiles.
Shover’s statement added company details not previously disclosed publicly. He described Zeus as built around a “Modular Seeker Interface,” letting operators swap the sensor package to engage different target types, and an “Open Warhead Design” that Aeon says can carry a 6-pound payload. He also said the missile can interface with “legacy systems” already fielded by the military, rather than requiring new supporting infrastructure, and that the company maintains a “transparent” bill of materials for the system, meaning it discloses the parts and costs that go into building each unit.
“When we speak to end users, Program Offices, Integrators, and Customers the message is clear,” Shover said. “Zeus fits into a giant gap that exists in the Defense Industry where a fresh approach has been needed for decades.”
Aeon has grown quickly since its 2023 founding. The company has raised $18.6 million in venture funding from investors including Quiet Capital, Silent Ventures and 1789 Capital, and it is relocating its headquarters and manufacturing operations from Austin to nearby Cedar Park, Texas, where the city council approved a $1.5 million economic development agreement in May tied to Aeon creating 135 jobs with a combined annual payroll of roughly $16.5 million by the end of 2029. Aeon has also moved beyond developing Zeus alone. In August, Tahmas hosted four congressional appropriations staffers for a tour of the company’s fuze production line, telling them Aeon would deliver nearly 1,000 fuzes the following week to support the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program, a roughly $1 billion push to buy more than 200,000 small, lethal drones by 2027.
That fuze work reflects a manufacturing strategy Aeon has applied to Zeus as well. The company has said it produces its own solid rocket motors and fuzes in-house rather than sourcing them from outside suppliers, a choice it frames as protection against the kind of supply chain disruptions that have affected larger, more traditionally structured defense programs.
Zeus itself is designed for both dismounted infantry use and mounted employment on manned and unmanned ground vehicles and surface vessels, with operators able to switch between roles by attaching or removing a shoulder mount, according to Aeon.
The company has said it holds an active integration partnership with one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers to enable Zeus to be fired from quadcopter platforms, along with a separate Ukrainian partnership covering integration onto ground vehicles and boats. The weapon’s targeting runs on what Aeon calls ODIN, a proprietary software-defined architecture the company says supports multiple targeting modes, engagement beyond the operator’s direct line of sight, and integration with battlefield command-and-control networks through the Android Team Awareness Kit, a mapping and coordination app used across the U.S. military.
Based on public contracting records reviewed by The Defence Blog in April, Aeon holds contracts worth eight figures with the Department of War for production and fielding of the Zeus system. The company has not disclosed the exact contract value, delivery schedule, or which military units or programs are receiving the weapon.

articles.title: Economic sanctions will also fail
articles.body:
The recent economic approach of the United States against Iran should be evaluated from several perspectives.
first, it should be examined why this action is being taken in the current circumstances which indicate that after six months, the Americans have not been able to achieve their set goals in the military confrontation with Iran; and that while they have used all their military power, put regional and trans-regional intelligence and security services to work, and have benefited from the capacity of hostile currents.
They have used everything they thought could lead to "Iran's surrender"; however, not only did they not succeed in imposing defeat or surrender on the Iranian people, but their actions led to disruption in the global economy and a surge in oil prices following the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz and its intelligent management by Iran.
In addition, they have suffered heavy military defeats that they themselves admit; They experienced unprecedented human losses after the Vietnam War and lost a large part of their regional military bases—which they had built at great expense, training troops, and transferring extensive equipment over many years—to the point that these bases were destroyed or seriously damaged.
Therefore, American statesmen are trying to hide their military failures under the guise of a new economic narrative and strategy; in fact, given the increasing domestic pressure from public opinion, the Democratic Party, and the US Congress against the Trump administration for imposing heavy costs on this country, they have entered the economic phase in order to escape these pressures and maintain their vote base in the upcoming elections, in order to divert public opinion from military failures through widespread propaganda.
 
 
 The second is to examine the possibility of implementing the announced sanctions; sanctions whose designers even stuttered and became ambiguous in response to questions from reporters. According to these sanctions, any country that has economic relations and exchanges with Iran will be subject to US sanctions. However, if the real capacity of the US to impose these sanctions is assessed, previous records show a different reality.
At the beginning of his presidency, Donald Trump announced in a threatening tone that the Panama Canal must be removed from China's influence and placed under US control, otherwise heavy tariffs would be imposed on this country. Then he imposed similar threats and tariffs against Canada, Mexico and other neighboring countries. However, today it can be seen that Washington's relations with Ottawa have become extremely fragile and the Canadian government has resisted these pressures; a country that has always been considered a traditional ally is now, with the support of its public opinion, resisting previous humiliating approaches.
In Mexico, these measures have also been ineffective, and the country has maintained its political and economic independence. Thus, the United States has failed to carry out sanctions and tariff threats even in its own neighborhood; on a higher level, the imposition of tariffs against China has also led to Beijing’s countermeasures; to the extent that Trump was forced to travel to China, and these tariff measures have harmed the US economy more than they have harmed China.
The imposition of tariffs against European countries has had a similar result; Washington’s hegemonic approach has caused the Europeans not only to not join in the measures against Iran, but also the NATO group to not join this campaign. This trend reveals the inability of the United States to impose its economic policies on other countries; now, in a situation where global dissatisfaction with US economic unilateralism has increased, the possibility of such plans against Iran’s success seems highly unlikely.
Third; If countries intend to join the sanctions against Iran, Tehran will also take countermeasures. Currently, the Persian Gulf countries have extensive trade exchanges with Iran; if the Strait of Hormuz is blocked, these countries will lose the possibility of trade and economic relations with outside the region. For example, the UAE is one of the major importers of food from Iran; as a result, the deprivation of imports from Iran, along with the lack of access to the Strait of Hormuz, will undoubtedly face this country with a serious crisis in the food supply chain, increasing inflation in this sector and harming other small industries.
On the other hand, China needs Iranian oil and has clearly stated that it will not participate in these sanctions. If the United States takes measures against Beijing, the Chinese side will take countermeasures; an action that is taken not only out of friendly ties with Iran, but also in order to protect its fundamental interests.
The situation in Russia is similar, and Moscow will never be burdened by Washington's imposed and sanctioned policies in the economic sphere. Other countries in the world also benefit from economic ties with Iran.
In recent decade, “national interests” have become the norm for governments, and countries are willing to protect their interests against pressure from major powers. The resistance of a country like Panama to Washington shows that even small political units are not willing to sacrifice their national interests for American interests.
Therefore, if Washington tries to confront all countries simultaneously to prevent economic exchanges with Iran, it will face defeat in the economic battle, just as it did in the military arena, and it must prepare itself to accept this defeat now.
The Trump administration came to power with the slogan of “America First”; a slogan that claimed to prioritize domestic interests, but in practice it has degenerated into an “America Only” approach; an approach that believes that only America has the right to prosperity and a decent life, and other international actors should simply execute its orders.
The international community did not accept this view, and as a result, the current stage has become one of "America alone" and isolation. In such circumstances, an isolated America will not achieve anything in advancing the recent sanctions policies.

articles.title: Anti-corruption probe hit Ukraine prosecutor general’s office
articles.body:
Anti-corruption probe hit Ukraine prosecutor general’s office
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) have exposed a criminal organization suspected of protecting a network of fraudulent call centers and laundering assets allegedly led by an official within the Ukrainian prosecutor general’s office, NABU announced on its Telegram channel.
This case is the latest in a series of high-profile graft investigations involving Ukrainian officials and figures close to Vladimir Zelensky.
Earlier in August, the Ukrainian leader sacked the deputy head of his office, Irina Mudraya. Her home had been searched searched as part of a probe into efforts to raise and legalize $3.3 million in bail money for former Energy Minister Herman Galushchenko, a key figure in a $100 million corruption case involving state nuclear operator Energoatom and linked to Zelensky’s longtime business associate Timur Mindich.
Other recent corruption investigations have targeted former Ukrainian ministers, diplomats, and senior officials. According to investigators, the criminal group was set up and headed in mid-2025 by a high-ranking employee of the prosecutor general’s office.
The official allegedly recruited serving prosecutors and associates into the scheme, all of whom regularly received bribes from fraudulent call centers in exchange for allowing them to operate without interference. The proceeds were allegedly laundered through the purchase of real estate, jewelry and other assets.
More than $500,000 was spent on real estate, valuables and other assets, while a further $300,000 in assets was concealed by transferring them to third parties. Another $250,000 was allegedly laundered through bank accounts, according to local media.
Five people have been detained as suspects and face racketeering and money laundering charges.
Sources cited by Ukrainska Pravda said Sergey Kropyva, head of the prosecutor general’s office cyber department, had already been detained as part of an operation code-named “Carthage.”
The investigative measures have also targeted Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, his deputy Maria Vdovychenko and Oleg Kiper, head of the Odessa regional military administration.
In August alone, anti-corruption authorities shut down hundreds of fraudulent call centers across the country, carrying out more than 400 searches and seizing more than $2 million during the raids.
The heads of NABU and SAPO recently warned that graft remains entrenched at the highest levels of the Ukrainian government. SAPO chief Aleksandr Klimenko said the state has repeatedly demonstrated that it has “no political will to fight corruption properly.”
Last year, Zelensky sought to bring the two anti-corruption watchdogs under tighter government control. He was quickly forced to reverse the move after it sparked nationwide protests and criticism from Kiev’s Western backers.
Moscow has long argued that the scandals reflect systemic corruption in Ukraine. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said earlier this year that corruption “permeates the entire Ukrainian power structure, including Zelensky’s inner circle and Zelensky himself.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s Lasar’s Group says its bomber drones destroyed rare Russian Zhitel jammer 55 km behind front
articles.body:
A Ukrainian National Guard unit says it destroyed one of Russia's rarer electronic-warfare stations, 55 kilometers behind the front. Lasar's Group said its own bomber drones hunted down an R-330Zh Zhitel jamming station near Sievierodonetsk in mid-summer, in a statement on its Telegram channel.
The Zhitel is worth the effort. It detects and jams GPS, satellite, and cellular signals, and Russian forces have been using it to blind Ukrainian reconnaissance drones over the Sievierodonetsk area. Mounted on a KamAZ truck, it can operate alone or be integrated into a wider jamming network, Militarnyi reported.
How the unit says it did it
The strike was the unit's own from start to finish, Lasar's Group said. Its intelligence analysts, working with the unit's aerial reconnaissance crews, pinpointed the Zhitel's exact position.
Strike crews then flew in-house-built LASAR bomber drones 55 kilometers deep to destroy it.
The rationale is simple: the fewer electronic warfare systems the Russians have, the freer Ukrainian drones are at the front, which is why such systems sit high on the Lasars' target list. The Zhitel they hit had been used mainly against reconnaissance drones, keeping Ukraine's forces from monitoring the area around Sievierodonetsk.
Not the unit's first
It is at least the second Zhitel Lasar's Group has claimed this year. In April, the unit destroyed a Zhitel and a command-and-staff vehicle in Kharkiv Oblast. The unit has made a specialty of hunting high-value Russian assets deep in the rear: in March, its drone crews tracked down a roughly $50-million Yastreb-AV counter-battery radar in occupied Luhansk Oblast, one pilot even landing a drone on the vehicle to follow it as Russian forces tried to move it to safety.
Taking out a jamming node like the Zhitel has an outsized effect: it restores freedom of movement for Ukrainian drones, brings back GPS-dependent navigation and weapons in the area, and makes it harder for Russia to blind Ukrainian reconnaissance.

There are fewer of them now, but a significant number are still being launched.

articles.title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
articles.body:
Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.
These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.
Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.
That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.
Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.
“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”
The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.
There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.
He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.
Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.
Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.
Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK.
The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count.
With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.
AI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.
Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.
Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.
The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.
OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.
The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.
OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.
“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”
His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”
And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.
He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”
